paragraphs.text: Chapter 4. Nutrition

Nutrition advice is everywhere, and it’s often conflicting. Eat meat. Don’t eat meat. Eat breakfast. Fast until noon. Carbs are the enemy. Carbs help you burn fat. Fats are key. Fats are bad. Sugar is poison. Calories, not sugar, are what matters. Seed oils are good for you. Seed oils are bad for you… It’s enough to make anyone dizzy.

And there are avid debates. While some get into nuanced biochemistry, others are surprisingly basic. For example, people still argue about whether the types of foods you eat are more important than how much you eat or whether protein guidelines are off by a factor of two. People also debate whether the timing of when you eat different types of food affects body composition—that is, your body fat to lean mass ratio. Worse, dietary fat and body fat share the same name: fat. That has millions of people avoiding certain dietary fats that, were they to eat them, would likely improve their health.

I’m old enough to remember the “low fat” trend of the early 1990s—when seemingly everything was labeled low-fat or nonfat, including things that never had fat in the first place, like soda and candy, but for which labeling as “no fat!” gave the false impression they would promote body fat loss.

I also remember the 40-30-30 carbohydrate-protein-fat ratio trend, too, which was good in principle, but difficult to adhere to because—at least in my opinion—it wasn’t restrictive enough to make it easy to follow. That’s right, it was too permissive to allow for easy decision-making about food choices. So people ate too much. They needed to be told what not to eat.
The point being: A clever way to start a diet trend is to demonize one type of food.

Which may partially explain why low-carbohydrate and ketogenic diets became popular in the early 2010s. Eating mostly just fat and protein requires some “no thank you” discipline but is otherwise pretty simple… until a few weeks in, when a person realizes that even a bowl of salad is off limits and that packaged “keto” snacks often contain a lot of calories… and that calories still matter.

The rise and somewhat-fall of keto seemed to usher in time-restricted eating, or intermittent fasting, which emphasizes extended periods each day (and night) with no food intake. This approach was attractive for people who find it hard to have “just a few bites” of a certain food yet find solace knowing they can eat that same food later, once they are in their “eating window.” But this diet can challenge even the most disciplined, because while it has practical, psychological, and some health benefits, it doesn’t work if people eat with abandon during that window. [^1]
Oddly enough, a reptile from South America entered the picture and settled one major debate. Yes, a reptile.
Long story, made short:
The Gila monster doesn’t need to eat very often. Just three to four times a year. A year!
A curious biologist asked why.
He discovered Gilas make a peptide called exendin-4 that potently suppresses appetite.
It was then discovered that humans make a peptide similar to exendin-4, called glucagon-like peptide (GLP-1).
Humans made drugs that mimic GLP-1, but a thousandfold.
People don’t want to eat as much and…
They lose weight.
And a trillion-dollar weight loss drug industry was born.

More importantly for this chapter, GLP-1s really did settle that major debate about why people gain, maintain, or lose weight. They proved that sure, you can argue about which foods may indirectly impact satiety, or which foods are healthiest, but when it comes to body weight, how many calories we eat relative to how many we metabolize matters.
And yet there is a lot more to nutrition. A LOT more. For health. For brain health too. And not just neuron health, but also for mental health. Even for our focus and ability to learn.

There’s a lot more to nutrition, in part because there are a lot of experts with different perspectives. True experts, who have done the research, observed what works or fails in the real world with women, men, kids, healthy and sick people, and with those who exercise and those who don’t, or just won’t.

I have had a closeup view of just how many perspectives are out there through my podcast. I’ve talked for hours with “pro-plant-based” scientists like Christopher Gardner, PhD, professor of medicine at Stanford University. [^2] I’ve learned from nutritional scientist Layne Norton, PhD, and nutrition educator Alan Aragon, MS, who draw from both their academic training and their experience working with thousands of people. [^3] I hosted osteopathic physician Gabrielle Lyon, DO, to discuss protein needs for both women and men, and endocrinologist Robert Lustig, MD, professor at University of California, San Francisco, about sugar. [^4] (P.S. Robert is not a fan of sugar!) Justin Sonnenburg, PhD, a microbiologist at Stanford and perhaps the world expert on the human gut microbiome, spoke with me about how to support a healthy gut with specific foods. [^5] Harvard Medical School psychiatrist Chris Palmer, MD, explained the now-demonstrated benefits of the ketogenic diet for depression and other mental health issues. [^6] And Satchin Panda, PhD, who directs the Regulatory Biology Laboratory at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies, in San Diego, shared his extensive knowledge on the science of intermittent fasting. [^7]

These experts disagree—sometimes vehemently—on many things… no surprise there. But they also agree about many things, and one foundational understanding in particular: that when it comes to body weight, how many calories we eat relative to how many we metabolize does matter.

In this chapter, you’ll learn the consensus from nutrition experts that you likely have not heard anywhere else. I’ll also share my own experience and observations, having tried many different approaches to nutrition. And I share one that is seldom discussed but that I, and many others, have used to great success. It builds on this consensus. It cuts through the noise. It puts you in the driver’s seat so you can make satisfying food choices that don’t sacrifice taste; that support your body composition goals; and that help ensure you get the macro- and micronutrients you need for brain and bodily health. And it can be done on a budget.
The Clean Omnivore Diet

I call the approach I’m suggesting here the “Clean Omnivore Diet.” As you’ll see in the pages that follow, this approach to nutrition is based in science. We begin, as we have for each of the topics in this book, with data. I provide an overview of nutrition to get everyone on the same page, and to help you navigate what follows. I do hope you’ll read it, because I know it will empower you, but I’ll understand if you’d like to jump to the protocols so you can learn what to eat and when for maximal health.
Body composition affects health and longevity. People with a higher ratio of lean mass to body fat tend to live longer than those with relatively higher percentages of body fat. [^8]

More than 70 percent of Americans are overweight and more than a third are obese, [^9] which basically means the majority of Americans are likely shortening their lifespan with their eating habits. The harshest messaging of this I’ve ever heard was from an MD colleague of mine who said, “You just don’t meet many obese eighty-year-olds.” Fill in the blanks on that.
Physicians are known for gallows humor, but this point matches the data. Body composition matters.

The advice for most people, given the above, might simply be “lose weight.” But that is short sighted. I said body composition, not weight loss. If you lose weight and much of it is muscle mass, your metabolism drops, and then it’s very easy to gain the weight back. (Muscle, if you recall from chapter 2, is very metabolically active, and plays a role in blood sugar management and therefore affects insulin sensitivity, which refers to how well your body responds to increases in blood sugar.) You need to maintain and/or increase muscle mass, along with bone mass, while you lose mostly body fat. And while bone is not as sexy sounding as muscle, having adequate bone mass and density is vitally important for your health and longevity too. [^10]

The not-so-secret secret solution? Do resistance training, and eat at what we call maintenance calories, or slightly submaintenance calories (300–500 calories less than you need per day—more on that in a moment)… unless of course you are among those trying to gain weight, in which case you want to eat a bit more (300–500) each day. In the short run, this works. But in the long run, everyone—not just those seeking to lose or gain weight—needs to eat for health and longevity, but also for taste, and in a way that is compatible with their social life, schedule, and budget. That’s a tall order.

The great news is that there’s considerable overlap among diets that do just that—and that includes the Clean Omnivore Diet. They won’t leave you avoiding restaurants, either. But they require understanding what food and nutrition are really about.
WHAT TO EAT

There are three macronutrients: proteins, carbohydrates, and fats. Each of these can be subdivided into categories according to how they are used by the body. Let’s take a closer look at each, one at a time.
How to Think About Protein

Dietary proteins are foods rich in amino acids, compounds that our body needs to make its own proteins. All the cells and tissues of our body—hair, muscle, bone, et cetera—contain those proteins. So we need amino acids from food to keep our cells and tissues functional. Of the twenty amino acids found in the human body, there are nine that we cannot make on our own; they must come directly from outside sources—namely from dietary protein. [^11] These nine amino acids are called the essential amino acids, and foods containing them are referred to as complete proteins. Many foods sourced from animals, such as red meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and shellfish, such as scallops and oysters, as well as many dairy products, contain all nine essential amino acids, and thus are considered complete proteins. Some plant-based foods such as quinoa, hemp seeds, and soy also contain all nine essential amino acids.

Most plant-based foods, however, do not have all nine essential amino acids and must be combined with each other to be considered complete proteins. Examples include beans with rice, or nuts with lentils. There is a lot of debate (of course) as to whether animal-based proteins are superior to plant-based proteins, but the debate is often misleading because it neglects a key feature of any protein. And that is what I will refer to as the complete-protein-to-calorie ratio (CP:C ratio). Even when comparing animal-based complete proteins to one another, it is important to consider their relative CP:C ratios. I’ll illustrate this concept by comparing some examples of different foods: 150 calories of chicken versus 150 calories of lean beef versus 150 calories of whole eggs versus 150 calories of tofu versus 150 calories of beans and rice. All are considered complete proteins.

Now, importantly, while you would need to eat beans and rice (or nearly any legume and any grain combination) to get all nine essential amino acids, these do not need to be eaten in the same meal to be utilized effectively. As long as you get sufficient essential amino acids across your meals over the course of a day, it works.
• 150 calories of chicken has about 28 grams of complete protein
• 150 calories of lean beef has about 25 grams of complete protein
• 150 calories of whole eggs contains about 13 grams of complete protein
• 150 calories of tofu has about 15 grams of complete protein
• 150 calories of beans and rice has about 6 grams of complete protein
• 150 calories of peanut butter on a slice of wheat bread has about 6.5 grams of complete protein
• And let’s throw in 150 calories of scallops, which has about 29 grams of complete protein.

The reason different foods and food combinations yield different amounts of complete protein at the same caloric level is because none of these foods are 100 percent protein. They also contain some fat, or in the case of plant foods, carbohydrates and fats.

Most animal-based foods like meat, eggs, and shellfish contain zero (or close to zero) carbohydrates, and varying amounts of fat. Dairy products contain protein and fat (unless defatted, like skim milk, for example), and dairy includes carbohydrates to varying degrees.
So we need to ask: Does a given “protein” contain all nine essential amino acids? And: What is its CP:C ratio?
In other words: How many calories of a given “protein” food do we need to eat in order to get enough of those nine essential amino acids?

The answer to that question matters for body composition, health, and the pleasure you experience from eating, because getting those nine essential amino acids is crucial for satiety. That’s because how much you eat at a meal is driven in part by your brain’s and body’s hunger for complete proteins. When you get enough complete protein, you tend to feel satisfied during, and for a long while after, the meal. When you don’t, you tend to feel hungry again soon after eating.

The nine amino acids are not the only reason we eat, but they are a big part of it. Below I’ll explain how, if we don’t get enough complete protein per calorie, we start to run into problems. Luckily, those problems are easy to fix. I’ll explain how to do that too.

I often hear: “But I eat protein! I eat beans, I eat peanut butter…” Well, neither of those are complete proteins, but if the beans are served with rice or if the peanut butter is spread on wheat bread, then they become complete proteins. Problem solved? Usually not. In fact, often it’s problem created. Remember, beans and rice together provide 6 grams of protein for every 150 calories. That means you would need to eat more than four times as many calories of beans and rice (700 calories) to hit the same amount of protein (28 grams) found in 150 calories of chicken. Peanut butter on wheat bread is a similar story, given that in those 150 calories, you’re only getting 6.5 grams of protein. That brings us back to CP:C ratio. Chicken has a high ratio; beans and rice or peanut butter on wheat bread has a low ratio.

To be fair, some animal-based foods also have a low CP:C ratio. Take most pork for instance. One hundred fifty calories of lean pork will give you about the same amount of protein as 150 calories of chicken or beef (about 25 grams). But most commercially sold pork products, such as bacon, ham, and pork chops, are not lean. Most contain a high percentage of fat, and often have sugar added to them too. One hundred fifty calories of low-sugar bacon has only about 10 grams of protein. Typical store-bought bacon with sugar added? About half that, at 5 grams. You would need to eat about 400 to 500 calories of bacon to get the protein found in 150 calories of chicken.

The takeaway here is that we need to prioritize eating complete protein foods, and we need to consider the CP:C ratio when selecting which to eat. While protein is not the whole story, the best nutrition plan typically places proteins with a high CP:C ratio at the center of the plate.
WHAT PROTEINS ARE BEST?

If you eat animal products, I suggest you prioritize lean cuts of beef, elk, venison, or bison, as well as fish and chicken. They have a high CP:C ratio. Many dairy products do, too, such as Greek and Bulgarian yogurt, and cottage cheese. Eggs are great as well, even though they do not technically meet the benchmark, given their ratio of protein to fat. That said, I still incorporate eggs into my diet most days. After years of public debate on whether eggs are healthy or unhealthy, the FDA consensus as of 2025 is that, yes, eggs are healthy. They appear on a list right next to salmon, 100 percent olive oil, fruits, and vegetables. [^12] Our grandparents were right (again!).

Powdered proteins such as whey protein have a very high CP:C ratio and are a convenient way to get enough protein for perhaps a meal or snack per day, maybe two if you’re on the go. But they should not be your only complete protein source because they lack a number of important vitamins and minerals and other micronutrients found in whole foods. You want to prioritize whole foods for that.

Plant-based sources of proteins, by contrast, tend to have a low CP:C ratio. So much so that it is best not to think of most plant-based foods as proteins at all. It’s more accurate to think of grains, like rice and quinoa, and legumes, like beans, simply as carbohydrates, because that’s mainly what they are. And think of the lipid-rich plant-based sources of proteins, like nuts, as fats, because that’s mainly what they are. There are exceptions, but by and large the CP:C ratio of these foods is just too low to consider them otherwise. Unless you’re burning significant calories through long-duration exercise or physical labor, relying on low CP:C ratio foods to try to get enough complete protein often leads to eating excess calories and putting on body fat. And for those trying to gain weight—yes, such people are out there—devote your additional calories to high CP:C ratio proteins, carbohydrates, and healthy fats.

And before you say “He’s an anti-vegan, ketogenic carnivore!” I assure you that is not the case. None of this is leading up to me suggesting a purely animal-based diet. I think vegetables and fruits are fantastic. I eat them daily and some grains too. Vegans who are willing to put in the work to seek out or prepare dishes with a variety of ingredients—such as beans and other legumes, rice and other grains, and tofu and tempeh—can get adequate amounts of the nine essential amino acids across the day without eating animal products. They just need to be mindful not to eat too many calories relative to their overall energy needs. I have seen a vegan diet work great for some people, but admittedly they tend to be very diligent about the sourcing and combining of their plant-based foods to achieve complete proteins. Or they do a lot of cardiovascular exercise—they run marathons, triathlons, and distance races of that sort—which comes with very high caloric needs compared to that of most people.

One more consideration as you select a protein source is the bioavailability of that protein source—how much protein you can absorb as you digest it, and then how much your cells can make use of it. There is ongoing debate about this amount. Classic studies concluded that we can only absorb about 30 grams of protein per meal. [^13] That amount became a sort of “law” of nutrition, especially in resistance training fitness circles that prioritize muscle protein synthesis—a process that is stimulated by weight lifting, but that is also involved in muscle maintenance for everyone, lifters and non-lifters alike. Later studies showed, however, that our bodies can use pretty much any amount of protein we ingest. [^14] What changed? Mostly the conversation around protein absorption.

A portion of the protein that we consume at any given meal is used by our muscles. But there’s a limit to the “dose” of protein our muscles can synthesize; that dose is around 30 to 50 grams at one time. [^15] Whatever amount we consume beyond that will be absorbed by the gut and the liver, and used for things like neurotransmitter production, hair and collagen growth, immune system function, and much more. (Note that for kids still growing, and for those who resistance train regularly, the amount directed for protein synthesis is probably closer to 40 to 50 grams per meal, with the excess available for other tasks.)

Does this mean that you must consume 30 to 50 grams of protein at every meal if you want to maintain your current muscle mass? Nope. Research on intermittent fasting (a good setting to investigate this question because daily calories are consumed in a small window rather than as three meals spread across a day) found that lean muscle mass is preserved as long as enough total protein is consumed in a day. [^16]

All of this explains why people versed in nutrition don’t just talk about how much protein we can absorb, but the metabolic fate of the proteins we eat. In fact, there are times when assimilating 100 grams (!) per meal is possible. [^17] Does that mean you should eat 100 grams of protein per meal? Not necessarily. First off, how many meals are you eating? And how much protein do you need? Again, we return to the data.
HOW MUCH PROTEIN DO YOU NEED?

Most people should aim to consume 1 gram of protein, ideally from high CP:C ratio protein sources, per pound of body weight each day. It’s not crucial that you eat exactly that much every day. I suggest it as a target from which you experiment a bit to find your protein needs. If you find yourself too full or otherwise unable to hit it, that’s okay. You should never feel like you’re force-feeding yourself just to hit a protein goal. Strive to hit the 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight (or close to it) most days. And if you prefer to divide your protein into multiple meals and snacks per day, do that. If, however, you prefer to eat twice a day and ingest more protein at those meals, do that, even if you’re resistance training specifically to gain muscle. While it’s true that spreading out your protein across four to five meals and snacks per day can provide a marginal increase in muscle protein synthesis if you’re resistance training and aiming to gain the maximum amount of new muscle, the difference it makes won’t be meaningful for the majority of people. So figure out the timing of your meals and snacks that works best for your hunger, energy levels, sleep, and schedule. Be mindful of, but don’t obsess about, that 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight target.

Some people worry that eating too much protein can cause kidney problems or gout, but the data show that only becomes an issue if people consume something in the vicinity of more than 3 grams of protein per pound of body weight—an absurdly high amount that most people would struggle to reach. [^18] So don’t fear eating high CP:C ratio foods. That’s one more debate that’s easy to settle.

Another debate: There is also talk that deliberately eating far less protein than we need can help us live longer. The theory is that eating protein stimulates a rise in the level of mTOR (which stands for mammalian target of rapamycin), a protein related to cell growth that, when suppressed, has been shown to extend lifespan in animals. [^19] So far, however, the data point to “NOPE” on whether a low-protein-to-suppress-mTOR diet helps humans live longer. [^20]

Entire books could be devoted to any of the topics above but for now, let’s just keep the CP:C ratio in the back of our minds as an important metric to consider when making food choices. Prioritizing eating enough foods with a high CP:C ratio to reach that 1 gram per pound of body weight removes a lot of confusion in the “what to eat” debate.
How to Think About Carbohydrates

Carbohydrates, or carbs, as we often call them, have become appropriately controversial in the last few decades. I say that because carbs include both healthy and very unhealthy varieties. And no, that’s not determined by just whether a carb is complex versus simple, a term that refers to their molecular structure (more on that later). Some carbs quell hunger. Others can make you eat with abandon. Sometimes it depends what those carbs are combined with. Carbs combined with fat and with sugar, for example, can make people with a sweet tooth feel like an addict who just scored: focused on getting more. It becomes very easy to overeat.

Should you just cut out all carbs? Well, cutting out carbs completely will make you lose weight fast, but mostly you lose water weight as carbs cause you to “hold” water. [^21] For most people, I don’t suggest suddenly cutting out carbs completely, though cutting back on certain types of carbs can be beneficial for many people. I’ve seen folks with autoimmune issues resolve them by moving to a carnivore (meat, salt only) or ketogenic (very low carb) diet. Then, most gradually reintroduce carbs over time, learning which carbs are problematic for them and which are not. I have also seen people who could not lose body fat do so on very low carb diets. Ketogenic diets have also been shown to be an effective treatment for some forms of drug-resistant epilepsy [^22] and in some cases for schizophrenia [^23] and depression. [^24] Also, some people just “feel better,” both mentally and physically, on a zero or near-zero carbohydrate diet. Incidentally, I am not one of those people. I love fruits and vegetables and I eat starches, but I am thoughtful about which and, to some extent, when.

I also know people who have done well on an “animal-based” diet, which recommends people eat only meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. It’s actually a misnomer because the actual animal-based diet made popular by Paul Saladino, MD, includes not just meat, eggs, fish, and dairy, but also fruits such as dates, bananas, cucumbers, and tomatoes (yes, those last two are fruits). [^25] This diet is much easier to adhere to, and arguably much healthier in the long run than a pure-meat carnivore diet. The controversial part is that it is ostensibly “anti-vegetables.” In the last year, I have seen public messaging from Paul that asparagus now gets the green light. (No pun intended.)

The low starch, minimal-to-zero vegetables thing can be a real challenge. The vast majority of us are—and want to continue to be—omnivores, meaning we would like to eat meat but also fruits, vegetables, and, yes, other carbohydrates. So with that in mind, let’s parse this category of macronutrients.

First, there is no such thing as an essential carbohydrate—you can survive by eating only proteins and fats. But all our cells run on glucose and, assuming we eat them, carbs readily get converted to glucose. That glucose is absorbed into our bloodstream—which leads to a rise in blood sugar, which in turn triggers the release of hormones like insulin that help manage this fuel. Typically, the breakdown of carbs into glucose is what our bodies prioritize for energy, then fats, and finally protein. That’s an oversimplification, but all things being equal, that’s the sequence.

To fully understand how carbs work, you need to know a bit more about how carbs are processed alone and in combination with other foods, and how they impact appetite. Carbohydrates can be broadly divided into complex carbohydrates and simple carbohydrates. Complex carbohydrates can be further (and still broadly) divided into starchy complex carbs and fibrous complex carbs. As a general rule, starchy complex carbohydrates, aka starches, are complex carbohydrates that completely or mostly dissolve in your mouth (after they are cooked or manufactured). Examples include rice, potatoes, beans, yams, pasta, lentils, bread, chips and crackers, and so on. When consumed with little or no added fats or sugars, non-processed starchy carbs are what some call clean starches. So if you’re wondering—chips and crackers, while mostly starch, are not clean. Although fairly calorie dense, clean starches like oatmeal, potatoes, rice, beans, and lentils are terrific sources of energy because they are more slowly converted to glucose by the body. Breads made without excess sugar or preservatives such as rye bread, sourdough, and unbleached wheat bread can also be considered clean(ish) starches.
That being said, you can overconsume starchy carbs. [^26] Four things tend to lead you there:
• If you don’t eat enough high CP:C ratio protein along with them.
• If you add sugar to them including jams, honey, syrup, and more.
• If you add fat to them like butter, oil, or cheese.
• If you add both sugars and fats.

Starchy carbs are easy to overconsume, in no small part because they literally melt in your mouth. They are flavorful especially when combined with fat and salt (think bread alone versus bread and butter with salt or bread dipped in olive oil with salt, or french fries, or macaroni and cheese). And when starches are combined with fat and sugar and just enough salt to bring out the sweet taste (think cheesecake, doughnuts, chocolate cake, pie, ice cream, and most breakfast cereals nowadays) most people find them super tasty, and hard to not overeat. Processed starchy carbs, like chips, crackers, store-bought cookies, frozen pizza, burritos, et cetera, are basically starches with fats and/or sugar blended evenly throughout, so every bite tastes identical—identically scrumptious that is. Chips and crackers are especially easy to overconsume because they activate the “eat more of this!” circuit in your brain and body, without any of the usual satiety promoting features of whole foods. They tend to have a very low CP:C ratio, and they are incredibly calorie dense for their size. You can easily eat 800 calories of chips without feeling full… and in many cases doing that will tend to increase your appetite. By comparison, you would have to eat about 16 ounces (a pound!) of cooked steak to get to the same 800 calories. I’m betting by the tenth ounce of steak, you’re going to feel very satiated, and would stay that way for many hours.

I don’t want to demonize starches. I eat them. I love them. Rice and pasta dishes and a great thick-crusted rye, or sourdough bread with olive oil or butter and salt are some of my favorite foods. I also think most people can enjoy a slice of cake or pie, a scoop of ice cream, a hot dog, a slice or two of pizza, and other carb-fat-sugar combinations now and again without any issue. But even if they are homemade, or from a bakery or restaurant that uses quality ingredients, they should not be a staple of anyone’s diet. And the packaged, processed versions are certainly damaging to our health. This is true for a variety of reasons, but their low micronutrient value and their tendency to make people overeat are just two. [^27]
SO WHICH CARBS SHOULD WE EAT?

Most people, unless following a ketogenic, carnivore, or animal-based diet, should consume some clean carbs one to three times per day. How much? A simple solution is to scale your starchy carb intake with the amount and type of physical activity you’re doing. Unless you are still growing, are very lean (less than 10 percent body fat for a man and less than 15 percent for a woman), or are doing a lot of cardio (1.5 hours or more per day on average) or hard manual labor (3-plus days a week), it is probably best to limit your starch intake to a third or less of your daily calories. Strive to make that from clean starches, and don’t add more than one to two tablespoons of fat (butter or olive oil, etc.) to any one starch serving. And don’t add sugar.

If you do intense cardio or hard resistance training three or more times a week (meaning you are doing compound multi-joint exercises and take your work sets to failure; see chapter 2 for details), then consider also consuming some clean starches in the meals that follow your training session. Ideally, eat some fruit too. Long, intense cardio and resistance training of the sort described in chapter 2 can deplete your glycogen reserves. [^28] You would be wise to consume 30 to 75 grams of high CP:C ratio protein in that same meal. By the way, unless it’s very intense, a yoga class or bodyweight workout won’t meaningfully deplete your glycogen reserves. Nor will half an hour of Zone 2 running or easy laps in the swimming pool. That is not what I’m talking about. But if you push yourself running, swimming, or cycling or training with heavy (for you) weights for forty-five to seventy-five minutes, or do a truly hard Pilates workout, then you likely need to replenish your glycogen reserves. Eating some clean starches (and fruit and some high CP:C ratio protein) is a great way to do that. In fact, unless you’re in ketosis and familiar with that state, failure to replenish your glycogen, or dropping your starches to zero for one to two days in a row, can lead to sleep challenges, headaches, and brain fog. Resistance training with any real intensity when you haven’t eaten any starches in the preceding days can be extremely difficult. Most need those clean starches, just not in excess. And if you resistance train with intensity—taking sets to failure or close to it (as described in chapter 2)—you’ll want to eat those clean starches to have the glycogen your muscles need to continue your workouts.

On that note, if you follow a ketogenic, animal-based, or carnivore diet, you’ll have to make up for the lack of starch with calories from fat and/or protein, and be mindful of replenishing your glycogen in other ways after hard workouts. Protein can be converted to glucose by your liver through a process called gluconeogenesis. I know very few people who consistently follow a pure ketogenic or pure carnivore diet who also consistently resistance train with intensity, but they exist. Shawn Baker, MD, a popular public educator and proponent of the carnivore diet, is a good example of someone for whom this approach works. I’ve seen a fair number of low/no-carb folks who do pull-ups and push-ups and other body weight exercises as well as cardio. But for most people, if you train with weights in a manner similar to how I described in Exercise Protocol 2, you’re going to want to eat starches, especially in the meal following training.

There’s another type of carbohydrate to discuss: fibrous carbohydrates, which as their name suggests, are high-fiber-containing carbohydrates like broccoli, cucumbers, lettuce, kale, chard, asparagus, and so on. These tend not to dissolve in your mouth, even if they are cooked first. It’s hard to overstate how great complex fibrous carbs are for us. Indeed, most of us should be trying to eat more of them. They are rich with vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients and, as their name suggests, they contain a lot of fiber. We’re told all the time that we need to eat more fiber, but trying to get fiber mainly from starches is a mistake. That tends to make people gain body fat, and I’m hearing from more and more people about allergy and gut issues due to eating too many grains. Look to get most of your fiber from vegetables. Though be mindful to chew your fibrous carbs well or they can be hard on your digestive tract. And it’s good to note if any specific fibrous carbs do not agree with you (you’ll know!). But as a general rule, ingesting more fiber from vegetables and from low-sugar fruits is associated with better health outcomes and longevity. [^29] Fibrous carbs also slow the absorption of glucose into your bloodstream for a steadier rise in your glucose levels, and they make you feel full. [^30] Our sense of satiety comes from a combination of having eaten enough essential amino acids and fatty acids, and from our glucose levels having risen (but not too high), but also from the mechano-sensation of the stretch sensors in our gut… which is nerd-speak for “feeling full.”

There are even more benefits. As I mentioned, vegetables contain remarkably high levels of micronutrients, like vitamins, minerals, and more, and deliver those with very few calories. Whether they taste “yum,” “yuck,” or “meh” to you tends to be a function of age (know many kids under eight that love chard?), and how these foods are prepared. It should be obvious that adding a lot of oil or butter or sugary sauces can quickly make fibrous vegetables easy to overeat, and very calorie dense—especially if the vegetables are cooked—so add those sparingly.

And we should all avoid fried vegetables, fried starches, and fried meats. Fried foods are terrible for your cardiovascular health and longevity and even have been linked to poorer mental health. [^31] They are high in calories, often high in sodium, and can contain trans fat, which has been linked to heart disease and other bad outcomes. If you’re serious about your health, ditch them. If you indulge occasionally with a doughnut or French fries, no big deal. But if eating fried foods is a daily, or even a weekly habit, it will likely catch up to you.
There’s one last carbohydrate relevant to this conversation. Simple carbohydrates are what are often referred to as sugars—although that can lead to a lot of confusion.

Unfortunately, when most people hear the word sugar they immediately think of white table sugar, or sucrose, but simple sugars exist in many forms. Naturally occurring simple sugars in foods that have fiber and fairly high water content, like fruits or vegetables, are absorbed more slowly. The simple sugars found in honey or maple syrup, which have very little fiber, and no fat, are absorbed very quickly. Lactose, the simple sugar found in full-fat milk, is absorbed slowly because of the presence of fat. The point is that sugars vary in type, and how fast they are absorbed depends on the other macronutrients (proteins, fats, and carbs) you eat with them.

Maybe you’ve heard that “sugar is poison.” This is not true of the sugar in fruit and vegetables, or in many full-fat milk products. If your goal is to have stable blood sugar and energy levels, those sources of sugar should account for about 95 percent of your sugar intake. And while you must be careful not to overconsume maple syrup or honey and other natural liquid sweeteners—they are very dense with sugar and calories—they are not poison. So adding a small bit of pure honey or pure maple syrup to your food or drinks every so often is no big deal.

Refined sugars are another story. Refined sugars are simple sugars that have been stripped of their fiber or fat content and are often chemically modified to taste extremely sweet. Some are so sweet that consuming them may change your sweet taste threshold and make otherwise savory or sweet tasting foods taste more bland. [^32] Luckily that effect is reversible if you cut out refined sugars even just for a few days.

Sucrose, which is refined from sugarcane, is the most basic example of a refined sugar. A bit of it here or there, like table sugar in dessert, is generally not a problem for most people. Keeping refined sugars to 5 percent or less of your sugar intake is a good idea. Or, if you loathe tracking that sort of thing, simply limit yourself to one serving—a scoop of ice cream or piece of cake—per week. To some of you that may seem spartan. To others, that may seem indulgent. Later we will discuss sugar cravings, and how to beat them. In the meantime, I can assure you that it is possible to stop craving sugar, and cutting out refined sugars entirely, or close to it, is the first step in that process.

Alas, these days, sucrose or high-fructose corn syrup are put into all sorts of foods that we think of as savory (e.g., soups, cereals, sauces, and salad dressings) in order to make them taste sweeter than they would otherwise. So be a bit more vigilant and read food labels if your goal is to avoid added sugars of any kind.

Sugar is immensely reinforcing—ingesting it makes you want to eat more. So while people debate if sugar is truly “addicting,” most everyone agrees that consuming refined sugars is highly reinforcing, and is not healthy—or at least offers little, if any, nutritional benefit. [^33]

So while I don’t think that sugar is “poison,” nor do I feel it meets the classic definition of addictive, which would mean its use is progressive and destructive to multiple areas of life, I do, however, think eating too many sugars, and especially refined sugars, is bad for us. It can lead to gaining body fat due to the overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value, as well as insulin sensitivity problems that, at the extreme, can cause diabetes and other metabolic issues. [^34] It can even lead to mental health challenges, such as depression. [^35]

And sugar is everywhere. Consider that complex starchy carbohydrates—like wheat, rice, potatoes—if refined to remove their fiber content become more like simple carbohydrates. Foods containing refined flours, such as bread, pasta, cereals, crackers, and most packaged snack foods, are good examples. And they often contain added sugar as well. Even if the packages show some amount of fiber, these foods almost always act more like sugars in the body—they get absorbed fast, and almost always lead to an overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value. While eating something fibrous (like a salad) or fatty (like almond butter) with these refined complex carbs will typically slow their absorption, the outcome is almost always the same: an overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value. I’m not out to demonize the packaged food industry but their goal is simple: to get you to buy and consume more of what they sell. And it’s clear they’ve been successful in reaching that goal given the prevalence of these foods and the declining health of those who consume them. We have plenty of evidence now linking ultra-processed foods with serious health issues, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, depression, and impaired sleep. [^36] The more cryptically problematic foods, in my opinion, are refined carbohydrates with added sugars. We don’t think of them as highly processed compared to, say, chips or microwave meals, but they are nearly as bad in terms of our propensity to overeat them. Luckily there is an easier and much more satisfying way to eat. One that is affordable too. But first, we have to understand fats.
How to Think About Fats

First off, it’s a real shame this category of macronutrients is called fats because that immediately makes people think about body fat, which almost no one wants. But you do want fats in your diet. Lipids would have been a better choice in my opinion but alas, here we are.

Fats are lipids, and they are calorically dense: 9 calories per gram compared to 4 calories per gram for carbs or protein. And fats are vitally important. We can’t live without them. In fact, a large part of each of our cells is made of fats, and thus consuming enough fats is crucial for cellular function and repair throughout the body. You need to eat fats, but the right kinds and the right amounts. So get it out of your mind that fats are bad. Remember, there are no essential carbohydrates, but you absolutely must eat protein and fat to survive.
Fats can be broadly divided into saturated fats and unsaturated fats.

The simplest way to recognize a saturated fat is that these are generally solid at room temperature. The saturated fat in cheeses and meats are good examples of this. While some non-animal sources such as coconuts and Brazil nuts contain saturated fat, most saturated fats come from meat, dairy, and eggs. People love to debate if saturated fats raise your cholesterol, and it’s become a circular argument because yes, they do, but then the discussion turns to if cholesterol levels, HDL and LDL (classically referred to as the good and bad cholesterols, respectively), are truly meaningful in predicting heart disease and longevity, or if there are more important metrics. The whole thing can get rather confusing. [^37] Some people who eat low saturated fat diets have high LDL, due to genetics or other factors like age; some people who eat high saturated fat diets don’t have high LDL, but they also tend to eat a lot of fiber, and not much starch and sugar. Pretty soon, talk turns to how insulin from carbs and not just fats impacts LDL… and the debate rages on.
SO HOW MUCH FAT DO I NEED IN MY DIET?

If you are eating animal-based proteins daily, and that includes eggs, red meat, or full-fat dairy, chances are good that you are getting enough saturated fat. If you are vegetarian or entirely plant-based, you might consider incorporating eggs and dairy (if vegetarian), along with coconut or coconut oil, macadamia nuts, cashews, or other foods and oils that have saturated fat.

Although debated, the data show that you want only moderate amounts of saturated fats in your diet because high levels of saturated fat consumption can increase systemic inflammation—an effect that is only made worse if you also ingest sugar. [^38] Some might argue that is a consequence of eating saturated fats and carbs, not the fats per se. Yet, even if you’re following a strictly ketogenic diet, excess saturated fat consumption is not good for your immediate or long-term health. [^39] So regardless of whether you are an omnivore, keto, or vegetarian, consuming leaner cuts of meat and emphasizing proteins with high CP:C ratios will help keep your saturated fat intake relatively low. It’s worth noting that I regularly do blood work to keep an eye on my cholesterol levels and other blood biomarkers. I think this is a good practice to truly understand how diet is affecting your blood lipids. Function Health, a company I’m an advisor to, makes this type of testing quite affordable. There are other companies entering the space as well and helping to drive the cost of blood tests down.
WHAT ABOUT UNSATURATED FATS?

Unsaturated fats tend to be liquid at room temperature. There are two types: monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, both of which come mainly from fish, seeds, olives, and avocados. (More on the benefits of unsaturated fats in Nutrition Protocol 5.)

And for those of you following the ongoing debate about seed oils—canola, grapeseed, corn oils, et cetera—I give my take on them in Nutrition Protocol 5. Some evidence points to the idea that if seed oils are used to replace someone’s saturated fat intake, their health improves. [^40] Though that overlooks the fact that consuming seed oils often tends to correlate with eating more processed foods, and carb-fat combination foods. And some argue excessive heat during seed oil processing makes them potentially hazardous, which is why this topic is contentious. (Nutrition Protocol 5 gives you a fuller picture.)

My recommendation is to save yourself a giant headache and when given the choice between cooking with seed oils or other fats, go with pure olive oil or avocado oil, or perhaps some small amount of butter, tallow, or ghee. If you need to cook at high temperatures, avocado oil is your best bet given that it has a high smoke point. Smoke point is the temperature at which an oil starts to smoke under high heat—which can lead to it degrading as the fats oxidize, and that produces harmful compounds linked to inflammation. When it comes to seed oils, I personally avoid them, opting to cook and make salad dressing from olive oil and using small amounts of butter here and there. No one debates olive oil’s health benefits. [^41] And it’s delicious.
THE BEST DIET FOR YOU

We have covered a lot here. But if you’re realizing that the use of words like proteins, carbs, sugars, and fats requires distinguishing the different types of each and how they interact, then you’re on track to devise the best diet for you. The good news: There are several different diet frameworks that allow for that, so you have options. Here they are:
Low Carb/Keto

Technically speaking, as discussed, we can get all we need to survive from consuming only proteins and fats, and can skip carbohydrates entirely. Done right, the ketogenic diet tends to raise energy levels and assist weight loss, because you excrete a lot of water that starches normally cause you to retain. Ketogenic diets have also been shown to help resolve symptoms of epilepsy, as mentioned already, as well as major depression, bipolar depression, even schizophrenia, in some people, and there is growing evidence it may help for people with gut and autoimmune issues. [^42] But to do it right means eating mostly fat, some protein, and very, very little carbohydrates, along with all the vitamins and minerals you need—which takes a lot of discipline and attention to detail. Most people just won’t do that for long because they can’t imagine saying goodbye to bread, fruit, pasta, salads, et cetera, forever. Still, it might be the right choice for you. Ask yourself this: Are you willing to give up starches and fruit?
Pure Vegan

By pure vegan, I mean no animal products whatsoever. That’s possible. A vegan friend of mine (yes, I have some vegan friends) is a “platinum star” vegan, meaning he’s never knowingly eaten any animal products. The real challenge with this diet is getting enough high CP:C ratio proteins without eating too many calories, and to make sure you don’t overconsume processed foods, just because many of them—such as French fries or coconut ice cream—are vegan (and convenient and delicious). I know people who have been vegans for many years and thrive. One thing all vegans must be careful of is muscle loss, especially as they age. Resistance training can help offset that, but getting those high CP:C ratio proteins is key, of course, too.
Animal-Based

This diet has a very misleading name, as, yes, it includes meat, eggs, and fish, but also fruit, honey, dates, tomatoes, avocados, coconut, hard cheeses, and other full-fat dairy. Sounds decadent, no? It is. But it also takes some discipline to follow because it’s an omnivorous diet minus any starches or vegetables. That means no rice, no oatmeal, no bread, no broccoli, no lettuce, and on and on. Yes, it intentionally lacks vegetables. And the only processed food you’ll eat on this diet is hard cheese like Parmesan. This diet is possible for pescatarians who want to eat fatty ocean fish such as salmon and sardines. It’s also fine for people who don’t like red meat but eat poultry. I have heard from many people who have achieved impressive body composition results and improved their health outcomes by following an animal-based diet. That said, because it includes a lot of calorie-dense foods, you still need to watch your total caloric and saturated fat intake. In my view, any dramatic effectiveness of this diet is likely to be multifactorial, including that it limits starch-fat and starch-sugar combinations, and that it makes no room for processed foods or refined sugars of any kind. It tends to quell hunger fairly well and contribute to stable blood sugar. That said, it can tend to lead to very high LDL levels in some individuals, which can be correlated with increased risk of heart disease and stroke, a result of fatty plaque building up in arteries. [^43] If you opt to follow an animal based diet, I suggest getting a calcium CT scan of your heart before starting and again a year later to see if it causes you to add plaque to your arteries. I know people for whom it has made plaque worsen, and those for whom (independent of their LDL levels) it has not caused increased blockages. We still have a lot to learn about the relationship between LDL, markers like ApoB, diet, and cardiovascular diseases. Meanwhile, assess your current cardiovascular risk profile and how your diet—animal-based or otherwise—is impacting it.
Clean Omnivore

My diet of choice is what I call the Clean Omnivore Diet because it checks off all, not just a few, of the key pillars of effective, health-promoting, delicious, cost-effective, and practical nutrition, which makes it easy to stick to. If we take a step back from the debates, and ask what we need and want from a great overall diet, the answer that emerges is this:

• Plenty of protein from high CP:C ratio sources: Aim for 1 gram per pound of body weight of high CP:C ratio proteins. Some days a bit more, some a bit less. If that feels excessive, and you find yourself dreading eating these foods, scale it back a bit.
• Plenty of fiber, vitamins, and minerals and micronutrients, from vegetables: 35 grams of fiber recommended for men each day.
• 25 grams of fiber for women each day.

• Healthy fats: Like olive oil, avocados, and maybe a bit from dairy like Greek or (my favorite) Bulgarian yogurt or nuts. Small amounts of butter are fine. Nuts and nut butters are calorically dense, and most people tend to overeat them, but assuming they contain no added oils or sugars (including cane sugar) they are also fine. (Read the packaging; manufacturers seem to sneak those into everything nowadays!)

• Fruit: Two to four pieces or servings per day depending on activity levels and caloric needs. Berries are a great choice, but expensive. Look for citrus, apples, peaches, and on and on. If you want to look up the sugar and fiber content of different fruit, do; opt for the lower sugar, higher fiber varieties if you can.

• Clean starches: Think rice, oatmeal, potatoes, yams, sourdough or rye bread, beans, lentils. The goal is to eat enough of these to fuel your brain and bodily activities, including regular moderate to intense exercise four to six days per week.
That’s what to seek out.

And not to sound like a broken record, but most people are best off limiting starch-fat combination foods and starch-fat-sugar combination foods. That means very little, if any, highly processed food like candy or cookies, boxed or frozen meals, or sugary drinks. Just cut them out. You’ll feel so much better in every way—not just in appearance, but your cravings for sugar will be greatly reduced.

If you want a decadent homemade or real bakery-made dessert, homemade pasta, or a couple of slices of pizza or ice cream now and again—as in up to once a week—no big deal (especially if you’re exercising as described in chapter 2).

Alas, there is no official name for this diet. While it’s pretty straightforward, it’s certainly not the Standard American Diet. Nor is it paleo or Mediterranean or animal-based. That’s why I called it the Clean Omnivore Diet. It’s clean, it’s healthy, and it’s satiating. It’s also flexible, meaning it works both for your preferences and your goals. For instance, at the end of this section I offer a suggestion that explains how one slight modification of this diet can allow for meaningful fat loss that you can maintain over time.

So aim for 30 to 50 grams of high-quality protein at each meal. That’s about one large chicken breast, a 6- to 8-ounce piece of salmon or other fish, or a 5- to 7-ounce steak. This will fill about a third of a standard dinner plate.
Fill another third of that plate with vegetables.

If you’re having starch with that meal, the starch can fill the remaining third of the plate. This is approximate. Don’t obsess. If you completed an intense resistance training session or a hard cardio training session lasting longer than forty-five minutes that day, feel free to increase the starch portion a bit. Otherwise, keep your starch intake moderate. [^44]
HOW MUCH TO EAT: CALORIES IN, CALORIES OUT

Whatever diet you decide is best for you, you’ll need to pay attention to how many calories you consume. Calorie is the unit we use to measure how much energy is in what we eat and drink. And the number of calories you consume versus the number of calories you burn determines whether you will gain weight, lose weight, or stay at your current weight. “Calories in, calories out” is the phrase to remember. Or, if you prefer acronyms, CICO. This is not a matter for debate; it’s a matter of thermodynamics.

If you want to lose weight, then you must consume (and absorb) fewer calories than you burn. I say “absorb” because not every calorie you consume is absorbed. Complete proteins are 4 calories per gram as they head into your mouth, but the metabolic requirement of processing those proteins ends up making them closer to 3 calories per gram when all is said and done. And while it’s not a dinner-table-appropriate topic, some of the calories in food pass through your digestive tract without being absorbed. For example, humans have engineered fats that improve the taste of a food, but that get eliminated from your digestive tract with no absorption of calories. Other calories fail to be absorbed because they have a rapid rate of passage through your digestive tract, or bind to fiber. But for the most part, calories eaten equals calories absorbed.
Which takes us to the calories-out part of CICO.

As covered in chapter 2, your basal metabolism is the number of calories you burn if you were to just lie in bed all day and night and do literally nothing. Contrary to what many people once believed, your basal, or resting, metabolism doesn’t change a whole lot with age, at least not after age twenty-five or so. [^45] Unless your muscle mass changes. If you lose muscle, your resting metabolic rate decreases. If you gain muscle, your resting metabolic rate will increase. This suggests that one reason people put on weight as they age is they lose muscle mass. Another is that as people get older in age, they tend to walk less and just generally move around less (even while seated!) and thus burn fewer calories each day. This kind of non-exercise movement, or non-exercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) in nerd-speak, may not seem important, but it is. It can burn greater than 1,000 calories a day in some people… so knee bouncers and fidgeters rejoice. [^46]

While NEAT is (amazingly) a key aspect to your daily caloric expenditure, you of course can’t get away with just fidgeting and walking. As explained in detail in chapter 2, exercise—specifically resistance training and cardiovascular training—is critical to maintaining healthy body composition over time. Also, if you are choosing to be in a calorie deficit to lose weight, and you resistance train, more of the weight you lose will come from body fat and less will come from muscle. If you don’t resistance train, you’ll lose roughly equal amounts of body fat and muscle.

The reverse is also true. If you’re in a calorie excess, you’ll gain weight that is a mix of muscle and body fat, but probably more body fat. That is, unless you resistance train, in which case you’ll gain more weight that is muscle, especially if many of the additional calories are from high CP:C ratio proteins. [^47] And if you resistance train while eating at maintenance levels, you’ll likely add muscle and reduce your overall body fat percentage. [^48]

So viewed purely through the lens of thermodynamics, does it matter what you eat? If you are thinking about total weight on the scale, then technically no, it doesn’t matter. A calorie is a calorie. But as you can see from everything we’ve discussed so far in the chapter, there’s more to it than that.
Physiologically speaking, we eat for four main reasons:
• To provide our cells with the raw materials like amino acids and fatty acids that they need to rebuild themselves
• To provide our cells with glucose to fuel their activities, that is, to give them energy
• To get micronutrients (such as vitamins and minerals) for our cells
• To provide sustenance for the beneficial bacteria that live in our gut
(We also eat for psychological reasons, but those reasons are countless in number: because it’s social, or it reminds us of home, or it reduces our anxiety, or it just tastes good, and on and on.)

That’s why I believe, given most people are (and want to remain) omnivores, that the healthiest possible way to eat is to get enough high CP:C ratio proteins, plenty of fibrous vegetables and some fruit, healthy monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, and a bit of saturated fat, too, and enough clean starch to fuel our brains and bodies. And to do all that without eating more calories than we need. It hits each of these four reasons, while helping us stick to the requirements of CICO.
A Word About Weight Loss, or the Clean and Lean Omnivore Diet

One of the best ways to avoid eating too many calories is to avoid processed foods entirely, while also restricting starch-fat and starch-fat-sugar combinations, even if the ingredients are not processed.

There is even a case for dropping starches entirely—at least for a while. I know it seems crazy, but I have a dozen or more close friends who really struggled with their weight for years who switched to a diet consisting of meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, fruit, olive oil, coffee, tea, and water (there’s an argument to be made that diet soda is fine to include too) and only used salt, pepper, and cinnamon for added flavoring. [^49] Without any calorie counting, they have lost anywhere from twenty-five to sixty pounds in four to six months, and kept it off. These friends also made sure to consume some low-sugar fermented foods each day, too, such as sauerkraut or kimchi, which promote microbiome health. All of them exercised but no more than they were doing prior to eating this way. Each reported “cheating” two to three times a year, usually for a holiday meal or birthday. They simply got right back to the plan the next day. And after a year or so of eating this way, the ones exercising regularly and intensely were able to start adding moderate amounts of clean starches, like potatoes, beans, and rice, back into their regimen with no detriment.

Their results were remarkable, but not atypical. Again, since the laws of thermodynamics are immutable, we have to conclude this diet naturally puts active people into a caloric deficit. What is wild is how fast it works, and how easy it is to stick to, and how it stands in bold contrast to their many other failed attempts to lose body fat in a sustainable way. You might say “No bread?! No ice cream?! No pasta?!” All I know is that the people who elected to eat this way report feeling very sated, which I attribute to the fact that they were getting everything their body needed physiologically and psychologically, without counting calories. And their improved body composition and other indicators of health, including sleep, just further reinforced their decision. I guess if we had to name this diet we would call it the Clean Omnivore No Starch Diet but that’s a mouthful so I’ve defaulted to calling it the Clean and Lean Omnivore Diet instead.
