STRAIGHT TALK ABOUT HIGHLY PROCESSED FOODS

It is true that eating 3,000 calories of highly or “ultra” processed food will not cause any more or less weight gain than eating 3,000 calories of non-processed food, but the damage the former does is real. Let’s acknowledge the one thing everyone in the nutrition field seems to agree on—the vegans, the carnivores, the keto enthusiasts, the vegetarians, and the omnivores: Highly processed foods are genuinely bad for us.

When we talk about highly processed foods, we’re referring to multi-ingredient, packaged products that are either ready-to-eat or only need to be heated up to eat. We’re not referring to single ingredient starches that just need to be baked or cooked in boiling water, like rice or potatoes or beans. That’s not “processing”; it’s “preparation”: And those are healthy, non-processed foods. Highly processed foods are problematic for many reasons related to our short- and long-term health. These products—even the ones labeled “Heart Healthy”—are often high in sugar, as well as various preservatives and artificial dyes that, while perhaps not deadly on their own, seem to pose a risk to health. [^50]

And recent studies suggest that eating a lot of processed foods can increase your risk of psychiatric illnesses, likely due to changes in brain metabolism. [^51] In fact, that is one reason why, as mentioned above, ketogenic diets (which are very low in carbohydrates) are increasingly being prescribed as a tool to improve mental health. Whether that is due to the absence of carbohydrates, the reduced intake of processed foods, or a direct effect of improved insulin sensitivity remains unclear, but the results are nonetheless compelling. We also have reliable evidence that diets low in fiber and high in processed foods, or even simply just high in refined carbohydrates, such as white rice and white wheat flour, increase the risk of cancer [^52] and cardiovascular disease. [^53] As do deli meats, which are effectively highly processed meats. [^54]

It’s hard to tack the health-degrading effects of processed foods to one aspect of their makeup. A study published in 2017 reported that nearly half of all deaths due to cardiac or metabolic issues are rooted in poor diet. [^55] The Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit organization, estimates that 678,000 US deaths each year are due to diseases stemming from an inadequate or otherwise poor diet. [^56] Half! Personally, I view highly processed foods as destructive to health mostly because of the other actually healthy foods you could be eating in their place. You still have to obey CICO according to your goals, and make sure you get the right macro- and micronutrients, but avoiding processed foods will likely add years to your life.
WHEN TO EAT

Then there is the question of when we eat. Here again, people debate. In the 1990s it became popular to eat four to six small meals per day, following a 1989 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine on the subject of “nibbling versus gorging.” [^57] The idea was that grazing throughout the day would prevent overeating in any one sitting and stimulate metabolism. It fell out of favor because it’s impractical. It also turned out to have a trivial impact on metabolism. [^58]

Most people default to eating three to four times a day, with one to two of those instances as snacks and the others as meals. Job, school, and social constraints usually dictate when, exactly, people eat.

The practice of time-restricted eating, also called intermittent fasting, as discussed earlier in this chapter, became popular a few years back, and many people follow this practice either deliberately or by default because they are not hungry in the morning. They end up restricting their eating to a window of four to ten hours each day, and most typically seven to eight hours. [^59] Some people limit themselves to one meal a day, which means their window is only one to two hours a day. There is now a fair bit of science—including clinical trials—on time-restricted eating. Intermittent fasting was made popular first as a way to lose weight and improve insulin sensitivity, meaning the extent to which our cells use glucose for energy (the more efficiently this happens, the less insulin we need to produce in order to regulate blood sugar levels). Soon it was studied and touted as a tool to live longer, to avoid cancer, and on and on. [^60]

When it comes to losing weight, the data show that intermittent fasting does indeed help when compared to “unrestricted eating.” However, it likely helps because people end up eating fewer calories when they limit their eating to a specific time window. So ultimately, it all comes back to CICO. When you put intermittent fasting head-to-head with a diet where people can eat whenever they want, but the two diets are matched for total calories consumed, the results end up being the same. A yearlong randomized study found that people with obesity who followed a calorie-restricted diet and ate only within an eight-hour window did not lose more weight or body fat compared to those who followed calorie restriction without the accompanying time-restriction plan. [^61] That being said, many people find it easier to control the hours in which they eat than to control the portion of what they eat, and thus find intermittent fasting a very effective tool for eating fewer calories than they would otherwise.

Many people opt for intermittent fasting because they incorrectly think that means you don’t have to think about the types or amount of food you eat, but if you care about your health you still do. Fasting doesn’t change our need for micronutrients.

Debate continues about what it can do. Intermittent fasting has generated interest for its potential to extend life. [^62] However, the only strong link between fasting and extended lifespan appears to be restricting calories, not meal timing. [^63] That said, Satchin Panda’s lab at the Salk Institute has shown that mice who eat across a twenty-four-hour window of time compared to an eight-to-twelve-hour window, even when calories are held constant, suffer negative health outcomes such as obesity, elevated glucose levels, insulin resistance, and fatty liver. [^64] Studies from Satchin’s lab have also shown similar adverse effects for humans. [^65] Further studies show that not eating within two to three hours of bedtime does seem to improve sleep quality, [^66] growth hormone release [^67] in sleep, and next-morning glucose regulation, [^68] all of which may indirectly impact lifespan. While restricting eating within two to three hours of bedtime does seem to be a best practice, there are some exceptions based on the type of meal. For instance, if you’re hungry and need a snack, consuming 30 grams of casein, the protein found in dairy, can help reduce blood pressure and perhaps even aid in exercise recovery, especially for those doing resistance training. [^69]

Some research suggests that time-restricted eating extends life because it increases autophagy, a process that removes damaged or used cells and cellular material from our bodies. [^70] We also know that extended fasting, such as consuming only water and electrolytes for one to three days, is linked to increased autophagy. [^71] But again here, it’s not the timing that increases autophagy; it’s the overall daily calorie deficit. [^72] And whether autophagy truly extends human lifespan is still unclear. [^73] Most evidence we have linking caloric restriction or intermittent fasting to lifespan is still largely from animal studies. [^74] Prolonged fasting in humans will no doubt improve certain health metrics, like insulin sensitivity, but it risks reducing lean mass. Exercise—both resistance and cardio training—stimulate autophagy but improve lean mass with the added benefit of improving fitness. [^75]

I reflexively do something similar to intermittent fasting. My first meal is typically around 11:00 a.m. or noon. I wake up at about 6:00 a.m. most days and I find it easy to wait to eat my first meal because I tend not to get hungry until 10:30 or so. Around 3:30 p.m. I usually get hungry again and I’ll have a snack. I prefer to eat my last meal of the day around 7:00 p.m., but I stay somewhat flexible on that depending on my schedule.

Since I’m typically done eating around 8:00 p.m., my eating window is usually eight to nine hours, maybe a bit longer. I’ve found that this slightly restricted window allows me to feel at my best while also helping me to manage my daily caloric intake.

From a health standpoint, it’s best to eat at fairly consistent times each day, [^76] but you don’t have to be neurotic about it. If someone sets a dinner time for an hour earlier or later than usual, or a bit outside your eating window, it’s not a huge deal.
WHAT’S AHEAD
The following protocols are not yet another trend to follow. When I said I hoped you’d find the best diet for you, what I meant is one that you can stick to.

These protocols are not complicated, they are not expensive, and they do not involve searching out obscure ingredients or creating an elaborate schedule of meal prep. They follow directly from the ideas discussed in this introduction to the chapter. Each explores a key point here, then offers one simple tool. My hope is that they will provide you with the inspiration and rationale to make easy yet meaningful shifts in your nutrition, and therefore immediate and long-term health. Adopting any of these into your daily routine can improve your digestion, your energy levels, and your ability to focus and concentrate. For those of you seeking dramatic positive transformations in body composition, I offer a sustainable way to do that too. Of course, exercise—per the recommendations in chapter 2—is critical for getting sustainable and healthy body composition changes, and exercise has its own benefits altogether. Some of the suggestions that follow will be familiar. Others may sound a bit heretical. But I assure you they work.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 1 90 Percent or More of the Food You Eat Should Be Unprocessed or Minimally Processed
WHAT TO DO

• Eat and cook with single-ingredient, non-processed foods. These include meat, fish, eggs, poultry, fruit, vegetables, rice, lentils, beans, oatmeal, pasta, olive oil, avocado oil, and even butter (albeit in small portions). They can be consumed alone or combined in recipes, and of course you can use spices, seasonings, and salt as well.

• Avoid ready-to-eat packed foods or packaged multi-ingredient foods. Most pre-packaged sauces and condiments should be avoided; these typically contain a fair amount of added sugar. Read nutrition labels to check.

• Consume nut butters in moderation. These can be healthy, but some contain processed oils and even added sugar. Even when nuts and salt are the only ingredients, all have a very high calorie-to-protein ratio. If you’re trying to lose body fat, then it’s best to abstain from nut butters entirely.

• Consume full-fat yogurt and cottage cheese and other forms of dairy, but in plain flavors only. Here too added sugars should be avoided. Add fruit, a drizzle of honey, or a pinch of cinnamon for taste if you don’t like these foods plain.
HOW IT WORKS

Food is amazing. Despite the debates, I think we can all agree on that. We eat for the building blocks food supplies our brain and body, as described in the introduction to this chapter, and of course for the pleasure of it. For many people, food is one of their biggest joys. I count myself among people who love to eat.

But the type of food we eat is probably second only to sleep and exercise for its importance to our long-term health. Centering our meal and snack choices on whole (that is minimally or non-processed) foods has so many benefits—disease prevention, longevity, cognition, mood, energy, reduced inflammation, healthy weight management, and more. The increasing concerns about processed foods stem from the plethora of data linking them to obesity, high blood pressure, heart disease, gastrointestinal disorders, cancer, and other serious ailments. [^77] Chemical additives used to color, preserve, texturize, and flavor these products have been linked to potential health hazards. [^78] Processed foods also tend to contain high amounts of sugar, even in products that would seem to not require it. And excessive sugar consumption is tied to diabetes, heart disease, cancer, and an increased risk of early death. [^79] All of which is to say, we need to make it a point to eliminate, or at least vastly reduce, processed foods.

The good news is that eating healthily is not complicated or expensive. We can all make incredible tasting meals and snacks using whole foods, if we learn just a bit about how to prepare them. Think: a perfectly cooked steak and carrots roasted with olive oil, salt, and some spices. In some cases, these foods need no preparation at all. Like a juicy orange or fresh berries. If these sound bland or overly simple, chances are your taste circuits in your brain and body need some recalibration.

If you have grown accustomed to eating processed foods, this recalibration can seem difficult. Processed foods alter our brain and gut to make us perceive other, more nutritious foods as less appetizing. It’s because of how sugar, certain starch-sugar, and starch-sugar-fat combinations are metabolized in our gut, and how they change our brain’s reward pathways. You’ll be happy to know, however, that the cells in your gut and brain are perfectly happy to rewire to make healthy, unprocessed foods literally taste better. It doesn’t take long, and it will make eating healthy most of the time reflexive.

This protocol looks at the gut-brain axis, the connection between the cells in our digestive tract and specific areas of our brain. That connection is the key to understanding how processed foods affect us.

Our gut talks to our brain via two main parallel pathways. The first involves the cells in our gut communicating with our brain using a neural pathway called the vagus nerve, a bidirectional superhighway linking the organs of our body and our brain. You may remember the vagus from chapter 3.

Our body and our brain are connected by a second pathway, through secreted hormones and small proteins called peptides (in general, the vagus pathway is the faster of the two). The hunger sensation arises, in part, because our stomach produces a hormone called ghrelin [^80] in amounts proportional to how much time has elapsed since our last meal. Ghrelin travels to our hypothalamus, a marble-sized brain region located over the roof of our mouth, where it activates our drive to seek food. [^81] Other hormones and peptides made by both our gut and our brain make us want to eat less; for example, the peptide GLP-1 gives us a feeling of fullness, which is why GLP-1 analogs are used as drugs to treat obesity. (The gut microbiome, the trillions of bacteria living in our digestive system, also influences hunger—more on that in Nutrition Protocol 6.) [^82]

At the same time, specific nutrients in the foods we eat—most notably sugars, but also fatty acids and amino acids—activate cells in our gut called neuropod cells that communicate with the brain via the vagus nerve, leading to the release of dopamine. [^83] And while dopamine does many different things in the brain and body, when it is stimulated in this context, it can drive the urge to consume more of that food. It’s an elegant mechanism if you think about it, because the taste of food in our mouth is not a great indication of the actual nutrients in a given food. Taste is more of a guess, a correlate. The cells in our gut, on the other hand, are poised to respond to the broken-down components of food, letting the rest of our body and brain know what we ate and what to eat more (or less) of. Amazingly, all this happens below our conscious awareness.

Given how sugar drives the urge to consume more, it’s no mystery why it’s in so many foods. Processed food manufacturers add sugar to foods so we buy and consume more of these foods. That’s why sugar can be found in everything from packaged mac-and-cheese to frozen pizza, and most everything else on the supermarket shelves. Even tortilla and potato chips can have added sugar. So does most store-bought pasta sauce. And salad dressings. And condiments. Which is why so many people crave sugary food all the time.
You get the idea. It’s a clever, albeit diabolical, tactic.

As mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, sugar that gets added to food is considered a simple carbohydrate. Typically it is added as sucrose, but sometimes as high-fructose corn syrup, or something similar. The exact form doesn’t really matter however. Our brains are hardwired to detect simple carbohydrates. Studies in both mice and humans show that even when we are unable to taste sweetness, we still show a strong preference for sugary foods and beverages, indicating that the brain can detect sugar by a pathway other than conscious taste. [^84]

Here’s a simple and fun experiment you can try; it’s something that Anna Lembke, MD, a world expert in dopamine and its role in craving and addiction, taught me. Eat one small piece of chocolate or one spoonful of your favorite ice cream. Both have sugar and fat, a combination known to trigger a lot of dopamine compared to eating either one alone. Pay attention to how it tastes, but then also notice your thoughts as you swallow. You’ll notice how quickly they move from “mmm, yum” to “I want more.” The immediate sense of craving that overlaps with pleasure is the power of dopamine in action. Sugar, in particular, amplifies that response, even after the flavor experience has passed, by activating the gut-to-brain pathway. [^85] It even works for sugary foods that don’t taste that good! And it’s why processed foods that we don’t even think of as sweet often contain added sugar.

Again, I want to be clear that I do not subscribe to the view that all sugar is inherently bad. A homemade dessert, chocolate, or ice cream once in a while… all can definitely fit within a healthy diet. But I do think we should limit these foods and avoid, as much as possible, consuming non-dessert foods that have added sugar, as well as any highly processed foods, except on rare occasions or out of true necessity.

Maybe you’re wondering about fruit, which as I mentioned contains a sugar called fructose. Fruit contains a lot of water, fiber, valuable nutrients, and polyphenols, compounds found in plants that have various beneficial properties. All these components contribute to the prevention of heart disease, cancer, and other serious health issues. [^86] And the high fiber content of most fruits slows down the absorption of sugar, which makes them less stimulating than desserts, sweets, or highly processed foods. But there are a few fruits that contain more fructose than others—like grapes. Note, too, that dried fruits, without their water content, now contain concentrated amounts of sugar. Fruit juices, like orange juice, are generally best avoided. They are high in sugar and calories, too, and the absence of fiber means that the sugar contained there is easily absorbed into the body, which means it spikes blood sugar quickly. Because that spike leads to a subsequent crash in blood sugar, [^87] consuming it often can lead, in the short run, to fatigue, sugar cravings, [^88] and, in the long term, an increased risk of diabetes [^89] and heart disease. [^90]

Then there are artificial and low-calorie sweeteners. The data show that artificial and low-calorie sweeteners do not drive the same craving typical simple sugars do. Stevia for instance, is safe, and may even have some health benefits. [^91] Aspartame appears to be safe too. [^92] Saccharin and sucralose, though, may negatively impact the gut microbiome. [^93] And there’s interesting data on diet sodas. In a randomized controlled trial from 2024, people who consumed diet sodas lost more weight than people who drank equivalent amounts of water. [^94] The underlying reasons include less hunger among soda drinkers and more cravings for sweetness among the water drinkers. At the same time, people who consume a lot of artificial sweeteners often experience increased overall appetite, perhaps due to glucose and insulin disruption. [^95] There isn’t a broad rule that applies to all artificial and low-calorie sweeteners. For some people, they seem to help with weight loss, whereas for other people, they stimulate hunger in ways that may make it harder to keep from overeating. You have to figure out which group you are in.

If a few diet sodas a day help quell your sugar cravings at a time when you’re trying to lose weight, then great. If you don’t like diet sodas, there is no reason to consume them. I drink beverages containing stevia and occasionally enjoy an aspartame-sweetened diet soda. When developing the zero-sugar cold brew yerba maté for Mateina (as noted, a company I partially own), I chose to include a small amount of stevia. I drink that for much of the early part of the day. I avoid sucralose and saccharin.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Do you have any suggestions for beating sugar cravings

Yes. Some are conventional; one is not (more on that in the last protocol of this chapter). As with many cravings, sugar can be hard to quit. If you think you’re overdoing it with sugar, then try committing to having no sugar for a certain period. I suggest one week. I promise that soon you will stop craving it so much, though it takes a few days to “get over the bump” (the heightened cravings) as they say.

Focus on consuming high CP:C ratio proteins, at least three times per day. And dietary fiber, mostly from vegetables and lower sugar fruits like apples and berries. If you crave chocolate, try and slowly develop a taste for raw cacao beans (five or six per day), which are rich in polyphenols, which again have various beneficial properties. Similarly, you can try 100 percent chocolate (not baking chocolate!). You read right. That’s no sugar, and no stevia either. It’s an acquired taste, but once people develop a taste for it, they generally like it. If you really struggle with sugar cravings, cut sugar out entirely but consider drinking a half tablespoon (about 3–5 g) of l-glutamine powder dissolved in water two to three times a day; this powder may reduce cravings by regulating blood sugar levels and thereby quelling the need for sugar. [^96] This is a somewhat unconventional tool—one for which we need more studies—but anecdotally speaking (about my own experience), it works.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 2 Stay Hydrated
WHAT TO DO
Regardless of what and when you choose to eat:
• Consume 18 to 24 ounces of water upon waking. Try to do this first thing in the morning before drinking or eating anything else, including coffee or other forms of caffeine.

• Aim to consume about 80 ounces of water across the first ten hours of the day. That’s about 2.4 liters. It is not necessary to consume 8 ounces each hour, but try to spread it out in a way that works for you. The earlier in the day you drink it the better. It’s typically best to avoid a lot of water in the hours before bedtime, since you want to wake as infrequently as possible to use the bathroom.

• For optimal performance during exercise, consume water according to this equation: Your body weight in pounds divided by 30 equals the number of ounces to drink for every 15 to 20 minutes of your workout time. This calculation originates with the work of human performance expert Andy Galpin, director of the Human Performance Center at Parker University, and is referred to below as the “Galpin Equation.” Example: Total body weight of 150 pounds ÷ 30 = 5 ounces every 15 to 20 minutes, which means 15 to 20 ounces consumed during an hour-long workout. You can sip water throughout, drink at regular or non-regular intervals. Your pattern of consumption during exercise will of course be dictated by the type of exercise you’re doing: running, cycling, swimming, et cetera.
HOW IT WORKS

Your body is made mostly of water. By one estimate, obtained by sending a weak electric current through the body, an adult human is about 62 percent water, with that percentage starting to decrease around sixty years of age. [^97] Water is essential for every biological process that we need in order to live and function. [^98] If there is one protocol that is most overlooked and that can immediately and significantly improve your energy levels, focus, and general feeling of well-being, it is this: Hydrate properly. It is rarely discussed. When we do hear about hydration, the message is typically a warning against dehydration, not the great benefits of hydration.
So let’s talk about what hydration is, and why it’s so powerful.

Hydration is the process of providing the cells of our body with the water they need for all those biological processes. Some hydration is achieved by breathing, some is produced through metabolism, and some comes through the foods we eat. Most hydration comes from the liquids we consume. The water we take in through eating and drinking enters our gut and is absorbed into our bloodstream and finally our cells.

Proper hydration is crucial to both the body and the brain. Hydration helps prevent injuries, improves recovery, and is also important for maintaining body temperature during and following exercise. [^99] It reduces the risk of kidney stones. [^100] Drinking water stimulates the sympathetic branch of your autonomic nervous system, the circuitry that increases your alertness and focus. (See chapter 3 for more on this.) Research indicates that drinking water can trigger the release of norepinephrine, the hormone that helps keep us focused and alert. [^101] In a study of fifteen children, proper hydration was tied to improved performance on tasks involving motor skills and memory. [^102] Similar findings have been observed in adults.

Dehydration, on the other hand, quickly becomes problematic. It’s also common. This is unfortunate because even slightly insufficient amounts of water in your body can diminish your concentration, alertness, short-term memory, visual perception, and other cognitive functions. [^103] Mild dehydration can cause low-level confusion, fatigue, depression, and irritability. [^104] One review found that a 2-percent decrease in body mass due to dehydration was enough to diminish mood, increase fatigue, and reduce alertness. That is remarkable because most people do not consume enough water to maintain hydration, and spend much of their day suffering the ill effects of mild dehydration… without even realizing it.

A mildly dehydrated state can reduce brain volume and alter the activity of neural pathways associated with motor output and cognition. [^105] It also reduces blood flow, which in turn diminishes the supply of oxygen to the brain. What’s more, it can cause headaches and lethargy, and of course a dry mouth and thirst. [^106] It’s important to note amidst all this that we can be dehydrated without registering thirst.

People engaging in intense exercise need to be especially vigilant about hydration, and not just in hot and/or dry environments either. In one study, eight trained cyclists rode for two hours on a stationary bike, consuming either 2.4 liters of an energy drink or 0.4 liters of water plus sports gel to equal the carbohydrates in the energy drink. The low-hydration riders became exhausted sooner and exerted less energy as they rode. [^107] In a study of seven experienced resistance trainers (all male), insufficient hydration decreased performance during exercise. [^108] These studies are small but are representative of what happens when we exercise.
The quantities provided in this protocol do not need to be followed to the precise ounce or milliliter. They are general guidelines to help ensure sufficient hydration.

One reason to focus on getting about 80 ounces of fluid in the first ten hours of the day is that this time is when our kidneys function at their best. Our kidneys filter fluid and produce hormones to regulate water and salt balance, among other things, and their efficiency at doing so is strongly governed by our circadian clock [^109] (see Sleep Protocol 1 for more on the circadian clock). Our kidneys are simply much better at filtering water and other fluids we drink in the morning and daytime than at night; their function tends to peak in midafternoon and is slowest around midnight. [^110] Focusing most of your water intake to the time of day when fluid filtration by the kidneys is at its most efficient will also help prevent, or at least reduce, having to get up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom, which is among the more common causes of sleep disturbance.

The quantity of 80 ounces across the first ten hours of the day gives us a solid metric to aim for. Simply make sure to drink 8 to 16 ounces of water (one to two glasses) upon waking, and again approximately every waking hour during the day. That will get you in the ballpark of 80 ounces in the first ten hours. Individuals living in hot environments tend to need more water. So do people who move around a lot, even if that’s in a temperature-controlled office or home.

But if you’re exercising, that’s where the Galpin Equation enters the picture. If you want to improve your exercise performance, hydrate according to this calculation. You’ll be amazed by the difference it makes. Again, anyone living in hot environments will tend to need a bit more water here too; so increase the amount from the equation by a few extra ounces every fifteen to twenty minutes.

Beyond these three points, just remember: Stay hydrated. Hydration sounds boring but it’s actually really powerful when it comes to improving health and performance and again, it’s one of the more overlooked tools out there. It’s important for your brain, for your skin and appearance, for your digestion, and for your mood. You will notice the difference in all these areas after starting to follow this protocol.
COMMON QUESTIONS
How do I know if I’m dehydrated

There are so many myths around this. Among the more popular ones is that clear urine indicates sufficient hydration. Wrong. Many factors impact urine color besides hydration status. Your urine can be yellow and you can still be plenty hydrated. Another: If you pinch the skin on your hand, it should retract in less than two seconds. Wrong again. This response depends on age, skin thickness, and other factors. It’s true that if you pinch the skin on the top of your hand and it does not return to its original state within three to five seconds, then there’s a decent chance you’re dehydrated. Same goes if your urine is much darker than usual. But that’s not the best way to guide your hydration, nor is whether your ankles are swollen… all of these are myths.
The best way to be certain that you are hydrated is… to not wait for some less-than-reliable marker to tell you so. Simply drink enough water.
Do I follow both protocols at once when exercising? In other words, do I drink the recommended amount during general waking hours plus the amount recommended for hydration during exercise

Yes. Drink the amount recommended for ten hours of waking, and add more using the Galpin Equation. If you don’t want to bother with the calculation, then just aim to ingest 80 ounces of water across the first ten hours of the day and add an extra 15 to 20 ounces of water for every hour spent exercising—and drink it while exercising.
Should I drink more if I’m someone who sweats a lot

People who tend to sweat a lot can increase the Galpin Equation by 50 to 100 percent during exercise. The same holds true if you are doing some kind of heat exposure that promotes sweating. For example, it would be appropriate to drink 8 to 16 ounces of fluid for every twenty to thirty minutes you spend in a hot sauna.

Electrolytes (particularly sodium, magnesium, and potassium) are also beneficial, especially if you are sweating. If you’re working or you’re exercising in a warm environment, or you’re spending time in a hot sauna, add a pinch of sea salt to water (and add a little lemon juice to offset the salty taste). Or use a commercial source of electrolytes to help replace those lost through sweat. I’m a fan of LMNT, a sponsor of my podcast, which has more sodium than most electrolyte formulas. (It also has zero sugar, which is good since many hydration formulas have added sugar.) Many people worry about salt intake but if you eat clean—meaning limited or no processed foods—there is a good chance you need more, not less sodium.
Even if I slow down my water intake after the first ten hours of the day, I’m still concerned about frequent nighttime waking. Is there a way to reduce this
It’s normal to wake up once during the night to urinate. To avoid waking more than once, try this:
• 1 Hydrate sufficiently during the day to ensure you are not excessively thirsty in the evening.
• 2 Reduce fluid intake in the evening (obviously).

• 3 If you do drink fluids (of any kind) later in the day or in the evening, sip them slowly. The rate at which fluid moves from the gut to the bladder is determined partly by the rate at which we drink. Gulping water quickly leads to sooner urination; sipping slowly leads to more time between urination. [^111]
That said, if you are still waking up often, that could reflect a bladder or prostate issue. Talk to your doctor.
I drink coffee, tea, diet soda, et cetera. Does that count toward my daily hydration needs

Technically, yes, but drinking good ol’ plain water is still important. Beverages containing caffeine act as diuretics; they stimulate urine production and therefore do not contribute to hydration to the same extent as non-caffeinated drinks. The amount of caffeine most people consume is usually not enough to cause significant dehydration, but anyone who drinks more than two cups of strong coffee per day—meaning more than 200 to 400 milligrams of caffeine—should make sure to drink at least those 80 ounces of water in addition, and perhaps as much as 100 ounces.

Keep in mind that many commercial coffee vendors brew their coffee strong, as in 300 milligrams or more of caffeine per serving. If you tend to feel shaky or lightheaded after drinking that coffee, you may be low on electrolytes, as caffeine causes excretion of sodium, a key electrolyte. I’ve known a lot of people who were able to eliminate caffeine-induced lightheadedness and shakes, and even the caffeine crash, by drinking a glass of water with a small pinch of salt dissolved in it, or by drinking water with a serving of electrolytes (sodium, magnesium, and potassium) alongside their coffee or other caffeine-containing drink. In fact, people who drink a lot of caffeinated beverages report that they feel much more energetic, and avoid the caffeine crash, when they are careful to also ingest some electrolytes before, alongside, or after their caffeine.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 3 Eat High CP:C Ratio Protein at Each Full Meal
WHAT TO DO

• Aim to include 30 to 50 grams of high complete-protein-to-calorie ratio foods at each meal or snack. Your daily goal should be around 1 gram per pound of body weight. This is the cornerstone of your diet.

• The number of calories from those foods will depend on what you select. Poultry, lean red meat, fish, and shellfish are the best high CP:C ratio sources of protein for those who eat animal-based products. Eggs are great as well, but they do have a relatively high calorie-to-protein ratio. Whey protein and plain full-fat Greek yogurt and cottage cheese too. Plant-based complete protein sources include beans and rice (together), lentils, soy, seitan, and some grains, such as quinoa. Just be aware that these have a less-than-favorable protein-to-calorie ratio.

• Nuts, nut butters, and most cheeses are not high-quality protein sources. And all of them are very calorie dense. Peanut, almond, and other nut butters are mostly fat, and most nut butters on the grocery shelf often also contain added sugar and/or seed oils. If you’re going to eat nut butters, limit them to a few tablespoons a week and be sure they contain only nuts and salt. No sugar or added oils. It would be better to avoid nut butters and eat whole seeds and actual whole nuts. But these are mostly fats; they are not high CP:C ratio proteins.

• If you are someone who tends to overeat, whichever foods you choose, eat your high CP:C ratio proteins first. Then any starches, then your fibrous vegetables. You’ll enjoy more satiety, better appetite regulation, and better digestion because apparently the French have it right about “salad last.”
HOW IT WORKS
I know it’s not much fun to see a delicious steak and think “amino acids,” but that’s what your body does. If you took apart any protein, you would find an array of amino acids.

As I explained in the introduction to this chapter, all living things need amino acids to make protein. The human body needs twenty different amino acids. Nine of these are impossible for our body to make on its own. We get them through the proteins we eat. The proteins that have all nine are considered complete proteins, and we want to consume these proteins, because the body uses them to maintain a healthy immune system, produce certain hormones, and maintain and increase muscle mass, among other functions. [^112] You might be amazed to learn that most of your organs, not just your muscles, are made of proteins that are remade every few weeks to months. And it’s these nine essential amino acids that allow for this to occur. Your spleen, your heart, your liver, your muscles—the protein we consume allows them to keep working as they should.

Your body is smart. While you might think you eat for pleasure, it’s actually how your body keeps you seeking the food it needs to maintain these processes—that is, seeking those nine essential amino acids.

Whole grains, vegetables, seeds, and legumes do not contain all nine amino acids, but it is entirely possible to obtain all nine by consuming a variety of these plant-based proteins. Whether you eat meat or not, you are foraging for amino acids as you choose your proteins each day. That’s why we feel so satisfied after we eat complete protein; it’s because the feeling of satiety is strongly linked to obtaining enough essential amino acids. [^113]

And there is one particular amino acid we prioritize in that foraging, even if we are not consciously aware of it. An expanding body of evidence indicates that leucine, one of those nine essential amino acids, is especially impactful. [^114] Rising leucine levels in a cell launch a signaling pathway associated with the protein mTOR (I mentioned it in the introduction to this chapter), which in turn triggers the body to make muscle. [^115] This amino acid also has several other known effects. Research has found links to improved immune function, for example, [^116] as well as increased muscle mass among older individuals. [^117]

As discussed earlier, mTOR has been linked with aging and cancer. One mutant strain of mice lived three times longer than usual after treatment with the drug that lowers mTOR, called rapamycin. [^118] But again, those results don’t appear to translate to humans, and in fact they have translated to far less dramatic results in normal mice. There is currently no evidence that stimulating mTOR has a life-shortening effect on humans. Rather, eating complete protein foods, and especially those rich in leucine such as lean meat, fish, and eggs, should be the cornerstone of your diet.
And not to belabor the point, but once again, we are less likely to overeat when we consume sufficient protein because it leaves us feeling full and satisfied. [^119]
COMMON QUESTIONS
Eating 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight leads me to gain weight and/or I don’t feel good. What should I do

Most people who strive to eat 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight do feel better than they did before adopting that habit. From time to time, though, someone will tell me they just don’t feel “right” eating so much protein, and that they feel that they must force themselves to do so, even if their overall caloric intake is in proper range for them. We don’t have the exact knowledge to know why that might be. I notice my protein hunger follows the intensity and amount of exercise I do, and while that makes sense based on how protein synthesis works, we don’t have any formal studies on training and protein hunger, so take my experience as what it is: anecdotal.

For those of you who struggle to eat 1 gram of quality protein per pound of body weight, there are a few things to consider: Make sure you’re eating high-protein foods without excess fat or preservatives. If that does not eliminate the discomfort, then try replacing about a fourth of your protein calories with clean starches, like rice, and with fibrous foods, like salad, broccoli, or apples, while keeping your overall calories approximately the same. Starches are calorie dense, so it won’t take much to offset the slightly lower protein intake. Then, make adjustments until you arrive at a way of eating that is sustainable, and makes you feel good.

CICO—calories in, calories out—is a universal law of nutrition. Well, that and we all do need adequate protein and essential fatty acids to survive (which is what this protocol is all about). Other than that, figure out what works for you. And what works best for you may even change over time. I have long made it a point to eat enough protein daily, but I need to eat more vegetables now than I did when I was younger to feel my best.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 4 Choose Fibrous Vegetables and (Some) Fruit as Your Major Sources of Carbohydrates
WHAT TO DO

• Vegetables should form the second major brick in the foundation of your diet and fruit, the third. If protein is the cornerstone, these foods build on it by helping to ensure enough vitamin, mineral, and other micronutrient intake.
• These foods are also essential for our fiber intake. Men should aim for at least 35 grams per day, and women at least 25 grams per day.
HOW IT WORKS

Many readers know already why vegetables and fruits are so important: They contain vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients like flavonoids, all of which our bodies need to function optimally. [^120] Once you understand how nutrient-rich vegetables and fruits are, you won’t think about them the same way again. Eating vegetables isn’t a chore; it’s a gift.

The fiber in vegetables and fruits is also important. [^121] A bit about fiber: It provides support structure for the plants that produce it, be that in the roots, the stems, or the leaves. And it’s the part we can’t digest when we consume them. Fiber can be insoluble (will not dissolve in water), soluble (will dissolve in water), or prebiotic (feeds bacteria).

We need all three. Insoluble fiber, present in root vegetables and fruits with edible seeds, helps with stool formation. Soluble fiber, present in foods such as avocados, carrots, and Brussels sprouts, collects waste products as it travels through the body, helping to eliminate them. Prebiotic fiber, present in apples, asparagus, onions, and garlic, provides sustenance for the beneficial bacteria in our gut microbiome, which promote intestinal health and also healthy brain functioning via the gut-brain axis. [^122] (The foods noted above are just a few examples from each category.)

And they do a lot more. Studies also indicate that dietary fiber reduces the risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of symptoms that increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. The heart-protecting benefits of fiber are widely known. A study that followed 9,776 US men and women for an average of nineteen years found that those who ate the least dietary fiber had a significantly higher risk of coronary heart disease compared to those who ate the most dietary fiber. [^123] A review of eleven meta-analyses, which each included several studies, confirmed the link between high fiber consumption and a reduced risk of several cancers, including ovarian, prostate, colon, breast, and pancreatic. [^124]

Consuming fiber can also leave us feeling full, simply from the physical bulk of the food in our gut and the slowed gastric emptying that results. [^125] It also leaves us less fatigued. That’s because consuming adequate fiber helps adjust what’s called the postprandial glucose response, the entry of sugar (and fat) into the bloodstream, which can otherwise cause “brain fog” and tiredness. Fiber also blunts post-meal inflammation that often follows eating a dish high in fat and carbs. That inflammation, in which levels of some proteins and hormones rise in the body, can contribute to the risk of heart disease if it occurs with any regularity.

How much fiber should we get? Men should get at least 35 grams per day and women 25 grams per day. Very few people actually do that. In fact, an estimated 95 percent of Americans do not consume recommended amounts of fiber. [^126]

Some people fear adding more fiber to their diet because it can cause gas and/or bloating. It’s true that a sudden increase in daily fiber intake may temporarily result in both. But once you’re eating enough fiber on a regular basis, this usually becomes a non-issue. In one study on the link between bloating, sodium, and a high-fiber diet, the researchers found that while this diet did increase bloating to some extent, an accompanying decrease in sodium lessened that side effect, pointing to the idea that it’s often what we add to vegetables that becomes the problem, not the vegetables themselves. [^127]
And at risk of sounding like your mother, vegetables require more chewing. You need to slow down and chew them well for them to digest properly, and for you to reap their full benefits.

A few notes on fruit: Some people find that eating fruit at the end of a meal causes some digestive discomfort. Others have no such issue. If you experience this problem, try eating fruit alone, before a meal, or as a snack rather than to cap off a full meal. It may help.

Beyond fiber, these foods contain, as I mentioned, essential vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients. The words vitamins and minerals are thrown around a lot (I did it above). But knowing which ones tend to be lacking in most people’s diets, and knowing how to get more of these from food, can make a real difference to our health. Magnesium is largely an under-discussed, beneficial component of many foods. This mineral, the eighth most abundant element on earth, [^128] is used by the body for energy production, bone development, making DNA, muscle contraction, nerve impulses, and even for regulating our heartbeat. [^129] In fact, it’s involved in more than three hundred systems in our body and thousands of crucial biological processes. Yet most people don’t get enough of it. It’s easy to rectify, and I’m sure you can guess how: by eating enough fruits and especially enough vegetables.

Studies of the so-called Paleo diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, lean meat, fish, eggs, and nuts (in other words, foods that likely reflect the diet of a hunter-gatherer living in the Paleolithic era) indicate that we once had a magnesium intake of about 600 milligrams per day, leading researchers to theorize that human metabolism is adjusted to this high level. [^130] Health authorities currently recommend 420 milligrams of magnesium daily for adult males and 320 milligrams daily for adult females. Available data indicate that most people consume less than that already low recommended amount. For Americans, the average is about 323 milligrams per day for males and 228 milligrams per day for females. This level is due, in part, to not eating enough foods containing magnesium, but likely also because many foods that would be high in magnesium are grown in soil depleted of this mineral due to modern farming methods. [^131] Major or persistent magnesium deficiency can cause heart problems, neurological problems, and also dangerous reductions in calcium and potassium. [^132] And we don’t know how moderate deficiencies over time may more subtly diminish our health and vitality.

Vegetables and some fish, such as salmon and mackerel, are excellent sources of magnesium. Avocados (technically a fruit) and certain dairy products, such as milk and cheese, also contain magnesium. Among the foods with the highest amount of magnesium are pumpkin seeds, almonds, black beans, and soybeans. And I know it can be hard to feel excited about kale, spinach, and chard, but a few minutes spent enlightening yourself about magnesium will likely change that. Dark, leafy greens are an excellent source of it and very low in calories; one cup of cooked spinach contains more than a third of the recommended daily intake and fewer than 50 calories.

And there are more vitamins and minerals that vegetables offer. Potassium (beets, tomatoes, butternut squash) is integral to muscle contraction and nerve impulses. [^133] Calcium (broccoli, kale, edamame, leafy greens) is crucial for our bones and our teeth. [^134] Flavonoids, a category that includes a wide number of compounds present in the plant world, can reduce inflammation; the risk of diabetes, heart disease, and breast cancer; antibiotic resistance; the formation of free radicals (atoms that can damage cells and can contribute to cancer formation); oxidative stress, which can contribute to various diseases and conditions including neurodegenerative disorders; and the risk of viral, bacterial, and fungal infections. [^135]

We could continue talking about the benefits of high-quality protein, vegetables, and fruits until the cows (and cauliflower) come home. In fact, cruciferous vegetables such as cauliflower and broccoli offer numerous additional benefits such as sulforaphane, which can help scavenge and detoxify endocrine disruptors and generally supports healthy reproductive hormones in women and men, [^136] and on and on. I hope that all we’ve covered in this protocol has inspired you to fill half your lunch or dinner plate with vegetables. Perhaps even add some spinach and tomatoes (though, again, technically a fruit) to your breakfast too.

Though one last note on fruit: Most people, unless they are very lean (less than 10 percent body fat for men and less than 15 percent for women) should probably not be eating more than three servings of fruit per day, especially if they are trying to lose body fat. Too much fruit, despite its fiber and water content, can stimulate hunger. Don’t get me wrong, fruit is amazing, and is always a part of a healthy diet. Enjoy it, but don’t overdo it.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Should I take magnesium supplements

I suggest turning to magnesium supplements such as magnesium bisglycinate or L-threonate before bed only as an if-needed sleep aid, as described in Sleep Protocol 9, and then only if you’ve tried all the other protocols in chapter 1. For the benefit described here, stick primarily with foods that contain magnesium as a source.

That being said, magnesium supplements can help us get our daily recommended amount of this mineral. Magnesium L-threonate and bisglycinate seem to avoid the issue of gastrointestinal distress that some people experience with this supplement. By contrast, magnesium citrate can cause gastric distress and can sometimes even act as a laxative.

For adults, a 135-milligram magnesium L-threonate or bisglycinate supplement daily before sleep may also help ensure you are obtaining the recommended daily amount. Or you can take it with dinner. Be sure to consult with a physician before adding any supplement into your routine.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 5 Consume Healthy Fats as Part of Most Meals and Snacks
WHAT TO DO

• Most of your fat intake should come from unsaturated fats. These are present in olives, avocados, olive oil, and avocado oil, among other foods. Cook with olive oil, and use it for your salad dressing. If you need an oil with a higher smoke point for certain recipes, avocado oil is a good choice.

• Consume omega-3 polyunsaturated fats. These are present in fatty ocean fish, like salmon with the skin, and in various fish oil and krill supplements. (More on the benefits of omega-3 in Nutrition Protocol 7 of this chapter.)
HOW IT WORKS

Perhaps no category of food is as feared, misunderstood, and maligned as fat. Part of the problem is terminology: The fact that we call dietary lipids fats brings to mind body fat. The two are not the same but they are easy to conflate.
I want you to create a healthy relationship with fat. The purpose of this protocol is to do that, based on science.

We all need some fat in our diet. The question is not if, but which and how much. Which? It turns out there are quite a few to choose from. And how much? As you learned earlier in this chapter, it depends on the other macronutrients you are eating, or avoiding, according to your overall diet (keto, clean omnivore, vegan, and so on).

And yet we have become wary of this macronutrient. This fear is based less on science than on history. Concerns about a link between fat and heart disease date back to the 1940s and grew in the ensuing decades. [^137] In 1990, the USDA Dietary Guidelines recommended that Americans limit fat to 30 percent or less of their total calories and saturated fat to just 10 percent of their total calories, a recommendation that led to a proliferation of low-fat and nonfat products. [^138] It soon became clear that these foods, often ultra-processed, were much worse for us than the fat we were now avoiding. These guidelines scared many people away from highly nutritious, high-quality protein foods that also contain some fat, like red meat and eggs. Moreover, we were then living without two crucial benefits that consuming fat provides: the way it slows the rise of glucose in the bloodstream and the way it increases satiety between meals. And Americans, on average, gained weight and suffered from rising rates of heart disease in the following years.

More recently, the pendulum swung the other way with rising interest in ketogenic diets, which involve eating mostly fat, some protein, and extremely few carbohydrates. [^139] Interestingly, this diet first originated as a treatment for some forms of epilepsy in the 1920s. It’s also been studied as a treatment for schizophrenia [^140] and bipolar disorder. [^141] As a daily routine, the ketogenic diet is hard to stick with. But this and similar trends helped spread the awareness that many fats, such as monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, are good for us.

How can we move forward? Again, by looking at the science. Though a comprehensive review of all types of fat is beyond the scope of this book, a few things are helpful to this discussion. Above we established that fats are made from fatty acids. The body breaks down the fat we eat into these component parts, which are then absorbed into the blood. Once inside the body, fatty acids contribute to the structure and function of cell membranes, help regulate metabolism, and influence hormone production, among other roles. [^142] Yes, dietary fat can be more readily converted into body fat, and it’s higher in calories per gram than carbs or protein—but at the end of the day, if we are burning as much or more of the calories we eat for energy to meet our metabolic needs, then it doesn’t matter if the calories we eat come from fat, carbs, or proteins.

We covered the main types of dietary fat in the introduction to this chapter: monounsaturated, polyunsaturated, saturated. There is also trans fat. A bit more detail on all is warranted. The terms saturated and unsaturated, and the reason the former are solid at room temp and the latter are not, have to do with their different chemical bonds inside the chains of fatty acids.

The lack of double bonds in saturated fats makes the molecules stack on each other more easily, which makes the fat more stable; this is why products like butter stay solid at room temperature. These fats are hard to digest, which can leave us feeling tired. They can also increase certain forms of cholesterol.

Unsaturated fats are kinked in their structure. When you want to consume fat, these are the ones to prioritize. They contain fatty acids, which trigger circuitries involved with many bodily processes mentioned above. [^143] Some fatty acids are directly involved in neuroplasticity, which we can loosely define as the continued ability to learn and form new memories and skills. [^144] Fatty acids are also integral to regulating appetite. The presence of fat triggers communication along the gut-brain axis, which prompts the brain to release chemicals that deliver a sense of satiety. In addition, fat in our body releases a hormone called leptin, which activates neural circuitries primarily in the hypothalamus that also result in the feeling of fullness. [^145] Leptin is also involved in the signaling pathways related to the menstrual cycle and sperm production. [^146] It is one reason why having enough body fat, but not too much, is needed for libido and fertility. It’s the signal from the body to the brain that food resources exist in sufficient abundance to potentially bring another member of our species into the world.

The fourth kind of fats, trans fats, are unsaturated, but the type of chemical bond is different from those in the other unsaturated fats. Although trans fats that occur naturally in some foods like meat and some dairy are relatively neutral or even beneficial to our health, when we hear about trans fats it usually refers to industrial-made versions. [^147] These types of trans fats negatively impact cardiometabolic health, and were banned from the US food supply in 2018. [^148] When you hear about partially hydrogenated vegetable oil, that is an industrial trans fat. Prior to 2018, many commercial products, such as margarine, processed meat, microwave popcorn, and packaged baked goods, made in the US contained trans fat, but no more. Health authorities recommend restricting industrial trans fats to 1 percent of total calories consumed—20 calories of a 2,000-calories-per-day diet, which is less than even one tablespoon. If you travel or live outside the US you’ll need to see if industrial trans fats are still used in foods there.

As I note in this protocol, ideally choose monounsaturated fats. Also include some amount of saturated fat. [^149] Although some studies have found that switching from saturated fats to polyunsaturated fats reduces the risk of heart disease somewhat, [^150] other studies have not confirmed this connection. [^151] And a common challenge that can arise when eliminating saturated fat from the diet is that it can lead to an increased consumption of ultra-processed carbohydrates and added sugar (we reach for a processed snack instead of, say, some cheese or full-fat yogurt), which is also detrimental to health. [^152] This often happens when someone decides to eliminate meat, and ends up eating more packaged foods to reduce the effort required to prepare high-protein meals. Ultra-processed foods often contain a lot of calories and little to no fiber. I believe it is better to have a little bit of satisfying saturated fat than to replace it with foods that do not trigger a satiety response from the brain, that the body cannot digest effectively, or that lead to overconsumption.

If you’re at this part of the protocol still wondering exactly how much fat to incorporate into your diet: Aim for 10 percent or less of your diet to consist of saturated fat. Keeping your overall fat intake to about 30 to 35 percent of your diet will help enable you to receive the benefits of this macronutrient without weight gain. Learn to love the right fats and your hormones, connective tissues, heart, and palate will all thank you.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Should I consume more fat on certain days or post exercise

No. Assuming you’re eating 30 percent or so of your calories from fat, and that fat is a mix of saturated fats from high CP:C ratio proteins, and otherwise unsaturated fats such as avocados, olive oil or avocado oil, and some nuts and seeds, there is no reason to spike or drop your fat intake. If anything, we need to increase our clean starch intake, not our fat intake, on days we exercise. That’s because intense exercise depletes us of glycogen, a sugar that the body makes as a way to store energy, which eating clean starch can replace.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 6 Consume Low-Sugar Fermented Foods
WHAT TO DO

• Consume two to four servings of low-sugar fermented foods per day. Eating foods like sauerkraut, kimchi, pickles in brine (that require refrigeration), kefir, low-sugar kombucha, miso, and natto supports a healthy gut microbiome, which in turn supports all your bodily functions.
HOW IT WORKS

The human microbiome—the bacteria that colonize our skin, mouth, digestive system, and the rest of our body—has become a focal point of both health research and health trends in recent years. Data from the Whitehall II study, [^153] which has been tracking the health of thousands of British civil servants between the ages of thirty-five and fifty-five since 1985, found that eating fermented dairy foods like yogurt and kefir reduced the risk of death, [^154] as long as coronary heart disease and diabetes were not present. In one surprising study of 710 people, consumption of fermented foods was linked to less social anxiety among those who were prone to it. [^155] That finding was correlation, not causation, and it’s impossible to know whether eating something like sauerkraut made people less anxious. But connections like these start to make mechanistic sense as we learn more about the microbiome.

Recent research suggests that our microbiome starts forming before we are even born. [^156] Bacteria we are exposed to during the birth process and in the early months of life continue to build this internal environment, which is then added to by microbes we take in through what we eat, what we drink, the people we come into contact with, the air we breathe, even the pets around us, and the soils we come into contact with. The specific makeup of our microbiome, including how diverse it is, changes according to our diet and our environment. [^157] Even exercise affects our microbiome. A review of twenty-eight studies found that moderate-to-high-intensity exercise done for thirty to ninety minutes at least three times per week, for at least two months, “is likely to produce changes in the gut microbiota.” [^158] The reason for this benefit is not fully understood, but may be connected to the changes our body goes through when we exercise, suggesting that temporarily being pushed out of our comfort zone is good for our gut diversity. [^159] Then again, we update our gut microbiome from all sorts of sources around us. The mere act of lacing up our muddy running shoes helps build our microbiome. I know that sounds crazy but that’s how the microbiome works: It’s an internal reflection of our interactions with the outside world.

Not all bacteria that enter our bodies take up residence in our gut. [^160] Some cannot survive the acidic environment, for example. Other bacteria cannot survive in areas with high oxygen concentration. And antibiotics tend to wipe out both the beneficial and detrimental bacteria from our gut.

And it’s important to have that beneficial bacteria present there. Studies have found connections between the content of our gut microbiome and many digestive disorders, such as irritable bowel disease and colorectal cancer.

The gut microbiome also appears to influence mood and mental health through the gut-brain axis (introduced in Nutrition Protocol 1). [^161] A 2022 review of twenty-four observational studies and nineteen experimental trials, totaling about four thousand participants, identified differences in the beta diversity—which measures how dissimilar the various bacteria types present are to one another—between individuals who had been diagnosed with major depressive disorder and those who had not. [^162] Researchers theorize that disruptions to the gut microbiome alter the release of serotonin and dopamine, setting off a cascade that ultimately ends with the release of cytokines, proteins that trigger the immune system into action and heighten inflammation. [^163] Specific inflammatory cytokines have been linked to depression. [^164]

On the positive side, we know that when our gut bacteria are provided with sufficient L-tryptophan (the amino acid precursor to serotonin) and short-chain fatty acids, they can readily help synthesize serotonin and signal for our brain to do the same, via our vagus nerve.

The Human Microbiome Project, the American Gut Project, the British Gut Project, and other ongoing large collaborative studies are continuing to uncover the function of the gut microbiome—both its role in healthy biological processes and its influence on chronic and acute ailments. Studies also seek to figure out which specific species of microbiota are beneficial and which are not. As a general rule, diversity is the most important feature of a healthy gut microbiome. [^165] Diet plays a huge role in ensuring that our gut hosts a wide range of healthy bacteria. [^166] Fiber has long been a focus in this endeavor to ensure a healthy microbiome (more about how to prioritize fiber in Nutrition Protocol 4). [^167] But fermented foods appear to play an equally if not more significant role as well. Hence this protocol.

Take the study led by Stanford University biologist Justin Sonnenburg comparing how dietary fiber and fermented foods affected the microbiome of thirty-six participants. [^168] Half of the individuals consumed a high-fiber diet for ten weeks, increasing their intake of soluble and insoluble fiber by eating more fruits, vegetables, legumes, grains, nuts, and seeds. They also consumed more vegetable protein and decreased the quantity of animal protein and salt. The other half upped their intake of fermented low-sugar foods like yogurt and kefir and also consumed fermented vegetables (sauerkraut, kimchi) and beverages (kombucha and vegetable brine). The researchers collected blood and stool samples before the ten weeks began, at four weeks into the intervention, and at the end of the following six weeks. The participants then began following a diet of their choice—maintaining their study diet or something else—and samples were collected after another four weeks.

Analyses of the blood and stool samples revealed that the group focused on fermented foods experienced a significant decrease in nineteen markers of inflammation, including the cytokines interleukin-6, interleukin-10, and interleukin-12b. The researchers also observed beneficial increases in the diversity of the gut microbiomes, as well as decreases in markers of immune system disruption in the low-sugar fermented food condition. The increase in microbial diversity was notably greater among the fermented foods group compared to the high-fiber group. This diversity lasted through the final four weeks of the study, after participants returned to the diet of their choice, indicating that the change was not due to a temporary passing-through of microbes but rather an “ecosystem remodeling,” as the researchers call it in their 2022 report in Cell.
COMMON QUESTIONS
What specific fermented foods should I eat

Any that require refrigeration and are low in sugar, and have no added sugars are good choices. Sauerkraut and kimchi are both excellent choices. However, take note that any sauerkraut, pickles, and such that are stable on the shelf have not been fermented and are not recommended. Kombucha is also great, though it contains small amounts of alcohol and is often high in sugar, and should therefore be consumed in moderation. Natto and miso, made from fermented soybeans, are also good choices and are widely available.

Many fermented foods can be expensive. Yogurt and apple cider vinegar are lower-cost items and easy to find in your grocery store. Kefir is a yogurt drink that is less common but carried by many markets, and also less expensive than some other fermented products.

It is possible to make fermented foods at home, but the process needs careful attention to avoid contamination with harmful bacteria or anything else that can cause a foodborne illness. Tim Ferriss offered a great protocol for homemade sauerkraut in his book The 4-Hour Chef, and that can also be found online. Pickling vegetables in miso is a relatively easy way to make fermented food at home. If you decide to make your own fermented foods, be sure to follow the recipe exactly, including all advised precautions.
I get an unpleasant histamine response from fermented foods—itchy eyes, tingling in my hands, and brain fog. What should I do

This is not uncommon. I’ve had this experience too from eating broccoli and onions, and I never knew why. When I hosted Sean Mackey, MD, PhD, and chief of the division of Stanford Pain Medicine, on the Huberman Lab podcast, he told me about his experience with gut pain, one that defied all approaches… until someone suggested he cut out histamine-containing foods like onions. [^169] I can live without onions, but love low-sugar fermented foods and the benefits mentioned above are motivation for me to eat them daily. But they can cause a histamine response. So I have taken the histamine enzyme diamine oxidase (DAO) before these meals. It’s inexpensive and it solved the issue for me.
NUTRITION PROTOCOL 7 Consume Fatty Ocean Fish and/or Consider Omega-3 Supplements
WHAT TO DO
• Make a point to consume some fatty, cold water fish once or twice a week. Consider including salmon with the skin, sardines, mackerel, or herring as part of your weekly diet.

• Take supplements of fish oil or krill oil, or, if you’re vegan, algae oil. Aim to consume 1,000 milligrams of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) per day. Some people will benefit from consuming as much as 2 to 3 grams of EPA per day, although for most people getting that 1 gram of EPA per day will suffice. Some may even wish to ask their doctor to prescribe generic or name brand Lovaza, which is high in omega-3 fatty acids (at 465 mg per capsule), and is purified of all metals and other toxins. It is now rather inexpensive to obtain given it is available in generic form. I take it daily.
HOW IT WORKS

Nutrition Protocol 5 included the somewhat bold suggestion that we build a healthier relationship with fat. The omega-3 fatty acids are among the best forms of fat. These compounds form polyunsaturated fats, which are found in some fish, some leafy greens, beans, many plant-based oils and some other foods. [^170]

As discussed earlier, fatty acids, the building blocks of fat, help with metabolism, how our bodies respond to hormones, physical performance, and more. [^171] The body can turn calories into stored fat. But we can’t make omega-3 fatty acids. We have to get them through our diet.

And we should make sure to do that because the evidence that omega-3 fatty acids are good for us—our brains, in particular—is persuasive. Research has found positive ties between omega-3s and memory, cognition, [^172] the maintenance of mental health and heart health, [^173] improved outcomes after heart disease treatment, [^174] and relief from depression. [^175]

Let’s get specific. Modern interest in omega-3 fatty acids can be traced largely to two Danish researchers who became curious about the diet followed by the Greenland Inuit. [^176] The low incidence of heart disease and diabetes led the researchers to wonder whether something in their diet, which contained large amounts of seal and whale fat, was staving off these illnesses. Their 1971 paper comparing plasma lipid and lipoprotein levels, which are associated with coronary artery disease, among a population of Greenland Inuit and a population of Danish citizens (including a small group of Inuit living in Denmark) led the researchers to speculate about a connection between the high content of unsaturated fat in the Inuit diet and low incidence of coronary artery disease as well as diabetes. The publication launched decades of research about the value of omega-3 fatty acids.

Omega-3 fatty acids have been studied in numerous disease settings, with varying results. Among the more striking findings, aside from the clearly beneficial role in reducing the risk of heart disease, is a link to the reduction of depressive symptoms. In one study, researchers randomized sixty people diagnosed with major depressive disorder to treatment with 1,000 milligrams EPA daily, 20 milligrams of the prescription drug fluoxetine (more commonly known as Prozac), or both for eight weeks. [^177] Among the forty-eight patients who completed at least four weeks of study treatment, EPA and fluoxetine were equally effective at treating depression, and the combination yielded better outcomes than either one alone.
I mentioned a few of these foods in Nutrition Protocol 5, but it bears repeating here for the particular benefits of omega-3 fatty acids they contain.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Fish oil supplements can be expensive. Are they necessary? Which ones are the best

Indeed they can be expensive and concerns about them turning rancid are real. To get 1 gram or more of EPA per day, make sure the source is fresh and from a reputable, third-party tested supplement company. The liquid fish oil (usually cod, mackerel, anchovies, or some combination) sold in dark bottles to protect from light is most cost-effective. Just be sure to keep the bottle refrigerated after opening or it can go rancid. As I mentioned earlier, these days I take Lovaza, which is a prescription high-dose omega-3 capsule that has been purified of metals and other contaminants. It’s available in generic form now so it is inexpensive, but you do need a doctor to prescribe it.
I don’t like fish oil or fish. Can algae or krill do the job for omega-3s
All these are decent sources of omega-3 fatty acids. For those who are allergic to fish oil or don’t want to take it for ethical reasons, algae oil supplements are vegan and rich with omega-3.
One warning: I know a fair number of people who tolerate fish oil well but for whom krill-based omega-3 gives them a rash that itches. I am one such person. So proceed with caution.
What about just eating a lot of fish instead of taking supplements

Again, it is hard to consume enough fish. High-quality fish can be expensive. We also have to be careful about avoiding mercury, which now exists in many species at levels that are too high for frequent human consumption. King mackerel, swordfish, and bigeye tuna are among the fish with the highest mercury levels. Cold-water fish with the lowest mercury levels and that are excellent sources of omega-3s include inexpensive options, like sardines and herring. These and supplementation are going to be the easiest and most cost-efficient approaches to follow. And maybe some sustainably sourced cod, tilapia, or salmon with the skin on one to two times a week, if you like the taste.
